I've read the full paper (Abramov-Maximov et al., "Multilevel Analysis of Oscillation Motions in Active Regions of the Sun," *Solar Physics*, ~2011). Here is my evaluation.

## The strongest quantitative claim

The paper's central quantitative result is the **~45–50 s delay between the radio (1.76 cm) oscillations and the optical (Hα) oscillations**, which the authors read as the propagation time of a magnetic-hydrodynamic (MHD) wave from the chromosphere up to the corona (the "CCTR"), yielding a coronal height of ~2700 km (45 s × the independently-measured ~60 km/s wave speed). This delay also underpins the paper's headline interpretation that the three-minute sunspot oscillations are a filtering/propagation phenomenon rather than a local cavity resonance.

## Audit of the evidence

**Is the comparison fair?** No — in a way the authors themselves flag, but which the headline result leans on anyway. The two signals being cross-correlated are fundamentally different observables:

- *Optical*: a one-dimensional line-of-sight velocity, measured only along the spectrograph slit, only the east–west (longitude) component, from the Hα line (chromosphere).
- *Radio*: integrated brightness-temperature variations at 1.76 cm (third harmonic of the gyrofrequency, ~2000 G, transition-region/coronal heights), summed over a ring/horseshoe source rather than a 1-D slit.

The paper states explicitly that "one cannot expect a strong symmetry in the oscillation process" and lists geometry (1-D velocity vs. integrated ring source), height-sensitivity, and projection as expected reasons for mismatch. Crucially, the two spectra **agree well only on one of the three observed days** (Aug 18, AR near disk center); on Aug 15 and 16 the radio and optical spectra disagree. So the single 45 s delay value that carries the paper's main physical interpretation comes from **one sunspot, one day, one viewing geometry, in a ~40–60 min time series containing only a few wave trains.** That is a very fragile basis for a universal physical claim.

**Are baselines current?** This is an observational solar-physics paper, so "baselines" here means the physical interpretation against which the delay is read. That part is reasonable: the ~60 km/s horizontal phase speed is taken from an *independent* measurement (their own prior H-inole work / Kobanov et al. 2008), and the MHD-wave-in-a-sunspot-tube framing is consistent with the cited literature (Lites 1992, Zhugzhda, Stauder, Brynildsen et al. 2002). The authors correctly note "to our knowledge" this is the first *simultaneous* optical+radio study of these MHD waves. So the physics baseline is not a liability. (The data are from 2004 and the toolchain — Torrence & Compo wavelets, Morlet 6th order — was standard of its era; nothing here has been superseded in a way that invalidates the claim, nor is anything claimed as state-of-the-art.)

**Are error bars / statistical significance reported?** This is the clearest weakness, and it strikes directly at the strongest claim:

- The 95% confidence level (2σ, 95%) the paper repeatedly cites is a significance test on the **wavelet power / oscillation detection** (via the COI), i.e. it says "these oscillations are not noise." It says **nothing about the uncertainty of the 45 s delay.**
- The delay is read off a single cross-correlation curve (Fig. 6d). That CCF is a **broad peak (~0.6)** over a wide plateau, produced from a very short record with only a couple of oscillation trains. **No error bar, no confidence interval on the peak location, and no false-alarm/significance estimate for the CWT coherence** is given. With only a few wave cycles, a shift of tens of seconds is comfortably within the ambiguity of locating such a broad, single-sample maximum; the "45 s" (vs. the abstract's "50 s," vs. the body's "40–50 s") is essentially a visual read.
- The derived **CCTR height (2700 km) and the implied wave speed** are products of that uncertain delay and separately-uncertain speed ("the actual velocity may be even higher"), with **no uncertainty propagation** reported. So the two most concrete numbers in the paper (45 s, 2700 km) have no stated error bounds at all.

## Verdict

A competent, well-executed observational study that applies a standard wavelet toolkit (CWT, CWT coherence, COI, 95% power threshold) to a genuinely useful simultaneous optical+radio dataset. Its real contribution is methodological. But the headline quantitative claim — the 45 s delay → MHD-wave propagation → CCTR height — is **under-supported**: built from a single observation on a single day (the only day the two modalities agreed), from a broad cross-correlation peak with no error bar, no confidence interval, and no significance measure, and with no uncertainty propagation into the derived coronal height. The physics framing is internally consistent and agrees with the literature, so nothing is *wrong*, but the quantitative leap from "spectra look similar and the CCF peaks here" to "MHD wave of speed X traveling 2700 km" is not statistically justified. The fair recommendation is to reframe the delay as a tentative, single-case indication and to report (or bootstrap) the uncertainty on the CCF peak.

### Scores

## The weakest link

**Location:** Section 4 (p. 9), the step where the measured 45–50 s delay is converted into a physical conclusion:

> "It is quite evident that there is a shift in time between them. The radio oscillations happen some 40–50 seconds after the optical… Therefore the delay of 45 sec is interpreted as the time of propagation of the MHD wave from the chromosphere to the corona and suggests that the height of the CCTR is approximately 2700 km."

This is the single step where the argument stops being entailed by the data. Everything else in the paper is handled with explicit hedges (the radio–optical similarity holds only when the AR is near disk center; longer-period modes are "low coherence"; the 16-min/32-min period ratio is "not exactly equal to 2"). The 45-s → MHD propagation-time → CCTR height chain is presented as established, but the number that drives it cannot support that interpretation.

## Exactly why this step fails

**1. The lag is measured between wavelet-power envelopes, not between oscillation signals.** The 45–50 s number comes from cross-correlating "power curves constructed by averaging the wavelet power across the frequencies 6.0–6.5 mHz" (Fig. 6c,d). Wavelet power is |W|² — a positive, phase-free, amplitude-modulation quantity. For the short, non-stationary, strongly bursty wave trains in this data, a lag between correlated envelopes constrains only when the two oscillations were *simultaneously strong*; it carries no information about the phase/group delay of the 3-minute oscillation itself. Two signals can have identical envelope structure with any phase offset — zero, a quarter period (~45 s), a half period — and produce nearly the same power cross-correlation peak. The paper *does* compute the cross-wavelet and wavelet coherence (Fig. 5), the quantities that actually encode relative phase, but uses them only qualitatively and extracts no phase lag from them. So the very instrument claimed to yield a propagation time is phase-blind.

**2. The two observables are different physical quantities from different heights and apertures.** The "leading" signal is the line-of-sight velocity of chromospheric plasma (a 1-D slit cut, LOS projection only); the "lagging" signal is the 17 GHz gyroresonance brightness temperature, ∝ T_e N_e, integrated over an extended ring/horseshoe source with a 10–15 arcsec beam. A delay between them does not identify a path or a direction of propagation at all. Competing, unexcluded readings include: (a) the coronal radio source responding to the same driver with a finite source-response/energy-transport time rather than a passing wave front (the paper itself notes the radio source "at the base of the solar corona is affected by this motion," p. 5); (b) differing spatial averaging of two non-co-located sources; (c) instrumental contributions from the 10 s integration/10 s map cadence versus second-cadence optical sampling.

**3. The delay is statistically marginal — and the paper concedes this about itself.** The underlying segments are 40–43 minutes with wave-trains only a few periods long, and Fig. 6d shows a *broad* cross-correlation peak reaching only ~0.7 over a width of order 100–300 s — the uncertainty bar is comparable to the 45 s peak itself. Most damning, in Section 5 (p. 12) the authors write that for the 8- and 15-min oscillations "the insufficient duration of the optical series… [makes] the estimate of the time delay of the radio oscillations with respect to the optical ones hardly reliable." That is the *same method on the same length of data* that produced the 45 s number. The paper therefore explicitly degrades exactly the step its headline quantitative claim rests on — an internal contradiction that should have demoted the height estimate, not left it untouched.

**4. The 2700 km arithmetic inherits further unverified assumptions.** Height = delay × speed presumes (i) the coronal/wave propagation speed equals the 60 km s⁻¹ measured in the *chromosphere* — a value the paper elsewhere ties to *acoustic* "visual pattern" motion, not to the MHD mode being invoked; and (ii) the 1.76 cm source sits exactly at the top of that column. A gyroresonance source in a ~2000 G field at 17 GHz (third harmonic) with T ~ 2–4 × 10³ K probably forms in the mid/upper chromosphere, lower than "the CCTR," in which case the 45 s delay would imply a much smaller height or a non-wavelike response rather than coronal arrival. No independent source-height calibration is attempted.

## What the data actually supports

The defensible claim is the modest one in the opening of Section 4: the 3-min and 5-min chromospheric oscillations and the 1.76 cm oscillation are coherent, share amplitude-modulation structure when the AR is near disk center, and their envelopes co-vary with a lag of order tens of seconds. That is a real and reasonably argued observational result. The identification of the lag as an MHD wave travel time — and the CCTR height of ~2700 km derived from it — exceeds what the phase-blind, short-train, marginally significant power cross-correlation can entail.

I've read the full 18-page paper (Ablamov-Maximov et al., "Multilevel Analysis of Oscillation Motions in Active Regions of the Sun," Solar Phys.). It is a classical observational solar-physics study comparing 2004 wavelet analyses of sunspot oscillations in Hα LOS velocity (Sayan Solar Observatory) with 17 GHz radio maps (Nobeyama Radioheliograph) for NOAA 10661/AR661. Below is my assessment of what is missing for an independent re-implementation.

## What the paper provides

- **Instruments & some observing parameters**: horizontal solar telescope at Sayan, Fe I 6559 Å (g=1.4) photospheric LOS velocity + Hα chromospheric LOS velocity, ~1″ slit resolution, east–west slit orientation, H₂O telluric-line correction of instrumental shifts; Nobeyama at λ = 1.76 cm, 10 s map cadence, 10 s averaging, 10–15″ spatial resolution.
- **Dates/times of the three optical intervals** (Table 1) and AR coordinates.
- **Analysis method specification**: sixth-order Morlet wavelets (Torrence & Compo 1998), cross-wavelet transform (Torrence & Webster 1999), 95% confidence (2σ) level, cross-correlation of frequency-averaged power curves at 6.0–6.5 mHz (citing Bloomfield et al. 2004), and a link to the standard Torrence–Compo wavelet code (pacos.colorado.edu).
- **Acknowledged data sources**: Mees Solar Observatory data (NASA grant NNG06GE13G) for Figure 1a/2a/3a panels, and funding references.

## What is missing — reproducibility blockers

1. **No code at all.** There is no repository, no scripts, and no description of the reduction or analysis pipeline beyond citing the generic wavelet package. The steps that actually matter — Dopplergram/background construction, subtraction of instrumental shifts via the telluric H₂O line, extraction of LOS-velocity time series along the slit, selection and averaging of the radio-specta region (e.g., the 24–25″ pixel used in Fig. 9), construction of the frequency-averaged power curves, and the cross-correlation — are unspecified. An independent group cannot reproduce the 40–50 s time delay without these details.

2. **No data availability.** The Hα/Fe I time series are proprietary Krasnoyarsk/Sayan data and are not deposited anywhere; no data-access statement, DOI, or archive link is given. The Nobeyama 17 GHz data are in principle publicly archived, but the paper doesn't identify the specific files/interval selection beyond Table 1. The "bright-source" radio selection criterion ("high brightness temperature and strong polarization") is qualitative — no threshold is given, so the source position/averaging region can't be objectively identified.

3. **Time-series reconstruction details.** Exposure duration and cadence of the optical spectroheliogram, the sampling of the radio time series, whether/interpolation performed to align the two series before cross-correlation, and the exact averaging bandwidth in each figure are not stated. These directly affect the ~50 s delay estimate.

4. **No uncertainty quantification.** The headline 40–500 s (≈50 s) optical-to-radio delay and the ≈2700 km CTR-height inference rest on a single cross-correlation peak (Fig. 6d), with no confidence interval, no lag-resolution error, no noise-floor estimate, and no significance test on the delay itself.

5. **Wavelet parameterization gaps.** Only "Morlet order 6" and the COI/95% contours are mentioned; minimum and maximum scale cutoffs, detrend/padding choices, and how the "wave-trains lasting >10 min" criterion was operationalized are not given.

6. **Geometry.** The slit orientation relative to the spot ("east–west, crossing the center") is qualitative; the exact slit centering in arcseconds and the spot reference are not tabulated, despite the optical-vs-radio asymmetry discussion depending on it.

7. **Items that don't apply.** Random seeds, compute requirements, ML prompts, and pretraining details are irrelevant — this is an observational-analysis paper, not a machine-learning one. No stochastic element is in the pipeline, so their absence blocks nothing.

**Net verdict:** The analysis rests on one active region, 40–60 min series, partly proprietary data, and an undescribed reduction pipeline. With the standard wavelet software cited, an independent group could rebuild the analysis *only if* the authors supplied the reduced time series (or raw data) plus the extraction/geometrical details above. As written, independent re-implementation is blocked.

## Scores

The concept — simultaneous optical + coronal radio wavelet comparison to measure chromosphere-to-CCTR MHD-wave delay — is presented as the first such optical/radio study of the 3-min oscillations; the method (wavelet cross-comparison) itself is well established and the result is a single-AR, preliminary measurement. The paper is sound and well organized but suffers from the reproducibility gaps above, limited sample, and missing error analysis.

# Critique: Writing and Framing of Abramov-Maximov et al., "Multilevel Analysis of Oscillation Motions in Active Regions of the Sun"

## Overclaims Beyond the Evidence

The paper's central empirical content is a cross-wavelet comparison of Hα line-of-sight velocity and 17 GHz radio flux from a **single active region** (NOAA 10661) on **three days**, with total observation windows of 40–60 minutes. Several sentences elevate this modest data set to broader physical conclusions it cannot support:

**1. The causal MHD-wave interpretation (Abstract + p. 9):**

> "A comparison of the wavelet spectra for optical and radio observations showed a time delay of about 50 seconds of the radio results with respect to optical ones. This implies a MHD wave traveling upward inside the umbral magnetic tube of the sunspot."

The word "implies" does enormous work. A ~50 s lag between two wavelet-transformed time series does not uniquely identify an upward-propagating MHD wave. Alternative explanations are not excluded: (a) different filtering heights of the *same* wave in the two formation regions could produce an apparent delay without a physical signal traveling between them; (b) a systematic instrumental or solar-cycle drift common to both channels; (c) the delay could equal a *downward* propagation if one mis-assigns the causal direction. The paper never quotes an uncertainty on the 50 s value, gives no significance test on the cross-correlation peak (Figure 6d shows the curve but no confidence band), and draws the result from one 42-minute interval. "Suggests a possible upward propagation" would be the honest phrasing.

**2. "Consequently this is certainly not a noise" (p. 4, §3):**

> "We calculated the cross-wavelet transform and wavelet coherency between optical and radio time series (Figure 5). Obviously the wave-trains of the optical and radio data agree well. Consequently this is certainly not a noise."

"Certainly" is an absolute. Coherence between two signals of the same solar object does not rule out (i) a common-mode instrumental artifact at the site, (ii) a spurious coupling through the analysis pipeline (both use the same Morlet kernel, same 95% FAP threshold), or (iii) a genuine oscillation that is *not* the MHD mode the authors attribute it to. The phrase "Obviously … consequently" is a rhetorical assertion, not a statistical proof. A single pair of observations cannot distinguish the intended physical signal from any correlated common driver.

**3. Deriving the CCTR height (p. 9):**

> "the delay of 45 sec is interpreted as the time of propagation of the MHD wave from the chromosphere to the corona and suggests that the height of the CCTR is approximately 2700 km."

The 60 km s⁻¹ propagation speed is borrowed from Kobanov, Kolobov, and Makarchik (2006) and is not measured in this paper. Multiplying an unmeasured speed by an un-uncertainty-quoted 45 s delay to claim a "height of the CCTR" of 2700 km conflates a model-dependent inference with an observational finding. Moreover, the CCTR height is spatially variable (thousands of km across a sunspot); quoting a single value from one event at one location over-generalises.

**4. The "first time" claim (p. 14, §6):**

> "To our knowledge, we present here for the first time the study of these MHD waves based on simultaneous optical and radio observations, which refer to coronal and chromospheric levels of the solar atmosphere."

The Nobeyama 17 GHz sunspot-oscillation literature (Gelbreikh et al. 1999, Shibasaki et al. 2001a,b — all cited in the authors' own introduction) had already studied *simultaneous* optical and radio sunspot oscillations. What is genuinely new here is the use of *wavelet coherence and time-delay cross-correlation* to extract a propagation delay. The "first time" phrasing overstates the novelty relative to what the authors themselves cite.

**5. The harmonic attribution of 16-min vs 32-min oscillations (p. 13):**

> "Although the ratio of the frequencies of the two modes is not exactly equal to 2 (about 1.9), the similarity of the temporal variations of the two modes lead us to the conclusion that the 16-minute oscillations are the harmonic of the 30–32-minute oscillations."

Acknowledging the ratio is 1.9, then concluding "the harmonic" anyway, is internally contradictory. A ratio of 1.9 (rather than 2.0 within measurement error — and no error on the period measurement is given) is equally consistent with two independent modes. The word "harmonic" implies a specific nonlinear generation mechanism that is not demonstrated.

**6. Grandiose framing vs. actual evidence (Introduction + Conclusion):**

The Introduction opens with "The study of oscillatory motions is one of the most significant methods of plasma structure analysis of the solar atmosphere" and the Conclusion says "This work illustrates the recent progress in a new approach." The study that actually appears involves one AR, three 40–60 min windows, a 1-D spectrogrograph slit, and a single radio source. The framing promises a field-advancing methodology; the delivery is one illustrative case. This gap between the abstract's general claims ("simultaneous observations in different layers") and the specific, single-event nature of the analysis is the paper's biggest framing problem.

**7. "It is well known" (p. 5):**

> "It is well known that most of oscillation processes observed in sunspots are unstable with a low level of the quality of oscillations."

No reference is attached to this sweeping generalisation. "Most," "well known," "unstable" are all doing load-bearing work without citation or quantification.

## What an Adversarial Reviewer Would Write in Their First Paragraph

> The authors present a wavelet analysis comparing Hα Doppler velocities and 17 GHz radio flux from the single active region NOAA 10661, observed over three nights of 40–60 minutes each, and interpret a ~50 s cross-channel time lag as direct evidence for upward MHD wave propagation through the umbral tube to a height of ~2700 km. I raise serious concern that the data cannot support this conclusion. First, the analysis rests on one active region and one primary time interval (2004 Aug 18); no independent repeat of the 50 s delay on another AR or even another day is offered, so the result is not yet a reproducible measurement. Second, no uncertainty is quoted on the time delay, the cross-correlation peak in Fig. 6d is shown without confidence bounds, and the authors do not test the null hypothesis that the observed lag could arise from (a) common formation-region filtering of a non-propagating oscillation or (b) instrumental or solar-activity common-mode signals. Third, the propagation velocity of 60 km s⁻¹ used to convert the delay into a CCTR height is adopted from the literature and is not measured in the present data; multiplying two uncertain quantities and calling the product "the height of the CCTR" is not a valid inference. Fourth, the paper's "first" claim is undermined by the authors' own citations (Gelbreikh et al. 1999; Shibasaki et al. 2001), which report simultaneous optical and radio sunspot-oscillation studies. Finally, the writing repeatedly substitutes assertive language — "certainly not a noise," "implies," "it is well known," "we lead us to the conclusion" — for the statistical tests that would actually be needed. In its current form the paper is best read as a promising first application of a wavelet-coherence technique to one event, not as a demonstration of MHD wave propagation in the solar atmosphere.

## Review — "Multilevel Analysis of Oscillation Motions in Active Regions of the Sun" (A. Abrahamov‑Maximov et al.)

### What the paper does
The authors compare quasi‑periodic oscillations (QPOs) in sunspots observed at two atmospheric levels of the same active region (NOAA 10661): line‑of‑sight (LOS) Doppler velocity in Hα (chromosphere, Sayan horizontal telescope) and 1.76 cm / 17 GHz gyrosynchrotron emission from ~2000 G field (chromosphere–corona base, Nobeyama). Using wavelet analysis, cross‑wavelet transforms, and wavelet coherence, they identify the 3‑ and 5‑minute modes in both channels, find the spectra agree best when the AR is near disk center, and report a ~40–50 s delay of the radio relative to the optical that they interpret as a ~2700 km ascent time of an MHD wave through the umbral tube — used to infer a chromosphere–corona transition region (CCTR) height. Longer 8‑, ~15‑, and ~30–32‑minute modes are also reported.

### Assessment
The **method is sound and the data are genuinely useful.** The multi‑level comparison (low‑atmosphere LOS Doppler vs. coronal‑field radio brightness) is a reasonable and fairly novel way to try to pin down where QPOs propagate, Morlet wavelets + coherence are appropriate for these unstable, short‑lived train oscillations (Fourier would be the wrong tool), and the 3rd‑harmonic gyrosynchrotron field estimate (≈2000 G at 17 GHz) correctly localizes the radio emission at the CCTR/base of corona. The conclusion that the 3‑minute mode is largely absent from the corona/CCP at the disk‑center umbra (no emission at the gyroradial harmonics) is a physically sensible explanation of the optical/radio discrepancy.

However, the **headline quantitative result is not robustly established**, and this drives my recommendation to *borderline*:

1. **Single‑epoch dependence.** The similarity of optical and radio spectra — and therefore the entire ~45–50 s delay and the CCTR‑height inference — arises *only* on 2004 Aug 18 (the one day the AR was near disk center). The other two days show no agreement, and the paper concedes this. A 15‑year Nobeyama archive plus Sayan runs is invoked qualitatively in the Discussion, but the reported number is a single point estimate. Fig. 6(d)'s cross‑correlation peak is broad (±~80 s), so "45–50 s" barely clears zero; the error bar is not quantified.

2. **Propagation vs. common‑source filtering is not disambiguated.** The delay of the radio brightness relative to the optical is attributed to a wave traveling *up* the tube. An equally valid reading is that the two observables (chromospheric Hα LOS Doppler and ~2000‑G coronal gyrosynchrotron) are merely formed at different heights with different filtering/phase responses to the *same* underlying mode. The paper leans on a cross‑correlation *lag of brightness*, not on wavelet *phase* / group‑time, and does not try to rule out the filtering explanation.

3. **Vertical‑velocity conflation in the height inference.** The 2700 km figure uses 60 km/s × 45 s, but that 60 km/s is the *horizontal* phase velocity measured in the umbra; it is simply carried over as the *vertical* propagation speed, which is not established. Inverting a height out of a delay that already depends on an assumed speed is circular‑ish; and the CCTR height is a property of the temperature structure, not something one reads off an MHD travel time. The acoustic‑ vs. MHD‑mode distinction (which controls the vertical phase velocity) is never made explicit.

4. **Thin theoretical linkage / scope and presentation issues.** The abstract promises local seismology, but the paper is phenomenological with no forward model or identification of the specific MHD branch (slow/fast, cutoff frequency) being tracked. Section 4 is titled "3–5 mHz" yet spans 3‑min through 30–32‑min oscillations — a real scope mismatch. There are typos ("minites," "32‑minute") and the key wavelet panels (COI cross‑hatch, contour legends) are hard to read.

### Recommendation
**Borders on borderline — I lean *borderline* (minor/major revision toward accept for a specialist solar journal).** The method, data, and multi‑level concept are defensible and worthwhile, and the paper is clearly accepted‑calibre for *Solar Physics*/*A&A*; but the central claim is single‑epoch and rests on an interpretive leap the data do not yet support.

**Score: 5 / 10**

### The three changes that would most improve the paper
1. **Establish robustness and error bars for the delay.** Extend the study from the single 2004‑Aug‑18 epoch to multiple simultaneous optical+radio days (from the existing 15‑yr Nobeyama archive + new Sayan runs), report the delay as a distribution, and propagate the cross‑correlation width (currently ~±80 s) through to the distance, so the CCTR‑height conclusion is either statistically supported or is explicitly demoted to a single‑event estimate.

2. **Disambiguate propagation from common‑source filtering, and fix the velocity argument.** Use wavelet phase/group‑time (not the brightness cross‑correlation lag) to establish the *sign* and *duration* of the lag; explicitly model/rule out the alternative that the delay is a formation/phase effect of two height‑different observables of the same mode; and decouple the *horizontal* 60 km/s phase velocity from the *vertical* propagation speed assumed in the 2700 km estimate (state the acoustic‑vs‑MHD mode and its expected vertical phase speed), so the height inference is not circular.

3. **Tighten scope, add a physical model, and clean up presentation.** Reorganize so the 3/5‑min and the 8/15/30‑min results get distinct sections (the "3–5 mHz" titling is inconsistent with the 30‑min content); add at least a simple forward description of which MHD mode is being tracked (branch, cutoffs, expected phase/frequency) so the wavelets are compared against a quantitative prediction rather than remaining descriptive; and correct the typos and improve figure readability (COI shading, contour legends, axis labels) so the central optical‑vs‑radio comparisons are unambiguous.

## Peer Review: *Multilevel Analysis of Oscillation Motions in Active Regions of the Sun*

**To the Editors** — Review of Abramov‑Maximov et al.

### Summary

The authors analyze quasi‑periodic oscillations (QPOs) of the sunspot in active region NOAA 10661 (August 15, 16, and 18, 2004) using simultaneous optical (line‑of‑sight velocity in Fe I 6569 Å at the photosphere and Hα in the chromosphere, Sayan) and radio (1.76 cm / 17 GHz, Nobe­yama) observations. They apply a wavelet transformation to both data sets, compute cross‑wavelet transforms and wavelet coherence, and compare frequency/amplitude features of the three‑, five‑, eight‑, and fifteen‑minute oscillations between the two wavelength ranges. Their principal physical result is a ~40–50 s time lag of the radio signal relative to the optical one (Figure 6), interpreted as an MHD wave propagating from the chromosphere to the base of the corona, implying a coronal transition region height of ~2700 km. They additionally report longer‑period (15, 16, and 32 min) modes from extended Nobe­yama data.

### Assessment

**Strengths.**

1. The core idea — simultaneous optical + radio wavelet analysis to bracket the same oscillation process at two atmospheric heights — is a reasonable and, to my knowledge, relatively unexplored use of the technique. The cross‑wavelet transform and wavelet coherence (Figure 5) are appropriate, and the 40–50 s phase lag with an upward‑propagating interpretation is a physically meaningful result.
2. The paper is honest about its own limitations (short 40–60 min optical windows, only the LOS velocity component, 1‑D slit scan vs. 2‑D radio ring, the dependence of optical–radio similarity on heliographic position). This candor is commendable.
3. The data quality appears adequate and the methods are well documented (Morlet wavelets, 6th order, 95% confidence / 2σ).

**Weaknesses.**

1. **Single‑event, statistically thin result.** The comparison rests essentially on the Aug 18 episode, where the AR lay near disk center. Two of the three days show poor optical–radio agreement. A single 42‑minute simultaneous record cannot distinguish a systematic propagation effect from a coincident modulation, and no error estimate or confidence level is given for the 40–50 s lag itself. The cross‑correlation (Fig. 6d) is shown over the full −300 to +300 s range, so a spurious shift within the short window is not excluded.
2. **Interpretation vs. measurement.** The step from "45 s delay" to "CTR height ≈ 2700 km" assumes a 60 km s⁻¹ phase velocity *and* that the delay is purely geometric propagation delay. But the observed lag could also reflect differences in the two filter functions (the paper itself concedes the Hα vs. cyclotron resonance filters narrow and shape the transmitted frequency bands) or in the source regions. The authors do not quantify this degeneracy.
3. **The longer‑period (15/16/32 min) section is under‑supported.** It is based on low‑coherence, short radio intervals, and the claim that the 16‑min mode is a harmonic of the 32‑min mode rests on a frequency ratio of 1.9 rather than 2, with the authors hand‑waving the difference as propagation dispersion. This is speculative.
4. **No comparison with competing models.** The conclusion leans on the "already accepted" MHD‑wave picture. A serious paper at this stage would at least discuss and argue against the closed‑resonator / magnetoacoustic‑gravity interpretation, which the introduction itself raises.
5. Minor: the abstract overstates the novelty ("a new method"), the wavelet‑COI cross‑hatching in Figures 3–4 obscures part of the near‑surface signal where the most relevant power sits, and several statements (e.g., "This certainly is not a noise") are too strong for the data volume.

**Minor errors / suggestions.**
- Clarify the meaning of "95% confidence level (2σ)" — 95% corresponds to ~2σ only under a Gaussian assumption; state this.
- Give the uncertainty on the 45 s lag and on the phase velocity.
- Justify the 4th‑order vs. 6th‑order Morlet kernel choice and check its effect on COI.

### Verdict

This is a competent, carefully presented observational study that makes a genuine (if modest) contribution — the simultaneous optical/radio wavelet comparison and the upward‑propagation estimate are new and useful constraints. However, it is built on a single, short event; the central physical claim rests on a single shift value with no stated uncertainty; and the longer‑period discussion is speculative. In its present form it is **borderline** for a leading journal: the method is sound, the execution is clean, but the significance and robustness of the inference are not yet at the level I would expect. I would recommend **major revision** focused on (a) error analysis of the time lag, (b) explicitly treating the filter‑function degeneracy, and (c) either strengthening or softening the CTR‑height and long‑period claims.

The work is scientifically sound but incremental in scope.

Here is my feedback on your work.

## Overall impression

This is a competent observational solar-physics paper. You have done real work — a genuine simultaneous multi-wavelength study that is uncommon, because it uses the Nobeyama radioheliograph (1.76 cm, coronal height) registered against chromospheric Hα LOS velocities, and applies a coherent two-sided method (Torrence–Compo wavelets plus cross-wavelet/coherence, with the Bloomfield cross-correlation recipe). The comparison of the *same* oscillation process at the chromosphere and in the corona is the paper's central value, and the geometry argument (similarity of radio and optical spectra appears when the AR sits near disk center) is a nice and largely self-consistent observation. For a first multi-level analysis paper, the structure, figures, and honesty about limitations are good.

That said, as it stands it reads as solid but underdeveloped, and the headline result is not as strong as you present it. Concretely:

## Main concerns

1. **The 50 s "time delay → MHD wave propagation → CCTR height" chain is circular and under-supported (your flagship result).** You write the delay "agrees well with the generally accepted idea that the three-minute oscillations show an MHD wave spreading upward." That is assuming the very propagation you are trying to demonstrate. A ~50 s lead/lag between two filtered, narrow-band signals can be produced without any propagating wave: differential band-pass/filtering of the same source, different source-formation heights for Hα versus gyrosynchrotron, the ring-to-slit geometry you yourself describe (1-D optical scan vs. integrated radio ring), or even a common driver with different rise times. You do not rule any of these out. Before claiming a 2700 km CCTR height, you need to argue the alternative (non-propagating) explanations away quantitatively, not just note "limitations of the method."

2. **The arithmetic doesn't tie down tightly.** You quote a 60 km/s phase velocity, a 45–50 s delay, and a "≈2700 km" height. 50 s × 60 km/s is ~3000 km; 45 s gives ~2700 km. Pick one and show the derivation. More fundamentally, this height is meaningless without a stated velocity model (which mode, what dispersion) and an error bar. A single point estimate of a CCTR height from one event is not a measurement.

3. **One active region, three short windows, one 42-minute optical/radio overlap.** This is the paper's biggest weakness. With one AR observed over three ~40–60 min intervals, your "systematic" findings — the disk-center dependence, the 8/15 min modes, the 2-minute lag on 5-min — are all effectively one example. You cannot support words like "the degree of similarity varies with the position of the AR" from N=3 windows of one AR. At minimum you should say this explicitly and downgrade the language; ideally you use the Nobeyama archive (which you mention covers 15+ years daily) to build a small statistical sample. Right now the statistical claims outrun the data.

4. **The 5-min result is weaker than the 3-min result, but sold at equal strength.** You show 5-min trains clearly in the optical but note only "only some" are identifiable in the radio. That is an important caveat that should be foregrounded in the abstract and discussion, not buried. The "similar spectral details in the umbra" claim rests on only one or two matched trains.

5. **No physical modeling, and it is acknowledged but under-motivated.** A 42-minute optical/radio overlap is short, yes, but that should drive a concrete plan: what specific quantity (a phase-velocity spectrum, a dispersion relation, the 3-min vs. 8-min phase split) would let you distinguish "upward MHD wave" from "filtered common driver"? The introduction promises progress toward local seismology and plasma-structure inference; the paper stops at cataloguing periods and lags. The Discussion needs to make the *next falsifiable prediction* explicit.

6. **Methodology is standard, not novel** (this is fine — you state it — but then originality should come from the physics, and currently the physics is thin relative to the methods). The cross-wavelet/coherence usage is textbook. The one thing worth emphasizing is your 95% (2σ) confidence treatment and the COI handling; make sure you're not over-reading features that sit on the COI edge (a few of the long-period trains in Figs. 3f, 5b sit close to it).

## Smaller points

- Abstract: "high level of instability of the oscillations in optical and radio data" — instability is not actually quantified; you measure frequency/amplitude drift and short train length. Say so.
- "Consequently this is certainly not a noise" (Sec. 3) — too strong from a coherence plot alone; cross-correlation alone could be coincidence of two noisy 1/hf sources. Soften.
- The claim that 15–16 min are a harmonic of 30–32 min rests on a frequency ratio of ~1.9 "close to 2." One ratio on one dataset is weak; note the alternative (two independent modes).
- Figure 7: the "phase lag ... quarter-period" statement is asserted as "common knowledge"; either cite it or drop it.
- Terminature: you alternate "MHD wave" and "acoustic waves" (Fig. 7 text) for the same phase-lag argument; be consistent about which mode you're discussing.
- The H₂O telluric correction and instrumental-shift subtraction are mentioned but not verified — a brief check (e.g., quiet-line baseline stability) would strengthen the optical data section.

## What to do next

(a) Get at least 3–4 additional ARs with disk-center crossings from the Nobeyama archive to test the position-dependent-similarity claim statistically. (b) Build the error-analysis for the 50 s delay and propagate it into the height; add a non-propagating null model. (c) Add one paragraph of concrete modeling (dispersion of kink vs. Alfvén vs. slow mode in a ~2000 G tube) so the 3-min identification is testable rather than assumed. (d) Re-scope the abstract to match what the data alone support.

This is publishable in *Solar Physics* as an observational/technique paper once the headline claim is made honest and a small comparison sample is added.

# Review of "Quantum interference and entanglement of photons which do not overlap in time" (Wiegner, Thiel, von Zanthier, Agarwal)

## Summary of the argument

The paper studies two-photon (second-order) correlations from two **independent single-photon sources (SPSCs)**—treated as two-level atoms with random emission times—detected in the far field. The authors show that:

1. The two-photon correlation $G^{(2)}$ contains a cross (interference) term whose visibility is set by the **indistinguishability** of the two-photon amplitudes, not by any temporal overlap of the individual photons.
2. For identical sources ($\gamma_A=\gamma_B=\gamma$) the visibility $V_c \to 1$ **independently of the detection-time difference** (Eq. 3), so a 100%-visibility two-photon interference can persist even when $t_2-t_1$ exceeds the single-photon coherence time $\tau_c\approx 1/\gamma$ and even the source-to-detector transit time $\tau_{TR}$—i.e., one photon is recorded before the other is emitted.
3. Inserting this into the CH74 Bell inequality (Eq. 6) and choosing $\psi_2 = \varphi_1 + 3\pi/4$ yields a **violation of the CH74 inequality** between two photons that never coexist.

The authors' conceptual explanation is that the far-field scheme plus the probabilistic emission erases the "which-way" (which-source) information: after the first coincidence the pre-measurement state of the second photon is the superposition (4), a "quantum memory," so the two-photon amplitudes stay indistinguishable regardless of detection time.

## What is strong

- **Clear, self-contained, and largely correct derivation.** The use of the quantum regression theorem to turn the master equation into the two-time expectation values (after Eq. 1) is clean and the passage to $G^{(2)}$ is straightforward. The paper is honest about the far-field, equal-coupling, and equal-frequency assumptions.
- **The central physical point is well made and correctly identified:** for independent SPSCs the relevant object is the joint (two-photon) indistinguishability, and for *identical* emitters the correlation visibility really is insensitive to the absolute detection instants. This is a useful, crisp way to state why "no overlap in time" does not by itself destroy the correlation.
- **Connecting the coincidence signal directly to a CH74 Bell violation** is a nice concrete payoff, and it is more than a hand-waving "entanglement" statement—the authors give an explicit inequality and angles.

## Points of critique

**1. The novelty of the core result is overstated relative to prior work.** The independence of the coincidence visibility from the *relative/absolute* timing for identical emitters is essentially the two-photon analogue of the standard "which-path erasure" argument and is close to the content of refs. 8 (Pittman *et al.*, PRL 77, 1917, 1996 — two-photon interference with a delay) and 9 (Cabello/Hong–Ou–Mandel with temporal separation). Much of the conceptual machinery the paper presents as new (indistinguishability rather than temporal overlap is what matters) is already the accepted message of HOM and of delay-tolerant two-photon interference. The genuinely new ingredient is specifically the *Bell-violation* framing, which is comparatively thin. The paper would be stronger if it more explicitly separated "known" (timing-independent $g^{(2)}$ for identical emitters) from "new" (the CH74 violation) and stated precisely which of the two claims is the contribution.

**2. "Interference" and "entanglement" are used somewhat loosely, and the paper doesn't fully defend it.** The "two-photon interference" here is really the presence of a cross term in $G^{(2)}$ arising from not knowing which emitter fired—closer in character to a single-photon which-path interference lifted to the two-photon level than to the antisymmetrization/anti-bunching interference of a genuine HOM dip. And calling the photons "entangled... even though they do not overlap in time" is interpretationally delicate: when the photons do not coexist it is not obvious that a well-defined *two-photon* bipartite state exists whose Schmidt decomposition one can call entanglement. The Bell argument is the safer claim, but the paper leans on the word "entanglement" in the title and abstract without a rigorous Schmidt-state argument for the no-overlap regime. I would like to see the authors either (a) drop the "entanglement" wording for the no-overlap case or (b) actually exhibit the bipartite state and its CHSH-violating correlators in that regime.

**3. The "which-way is really erased" point deserves more scrutiny than it receives.** The authors' argument is that the post-first-detection state (4) is a coherent superposition, so the timing does not reveal the source. But there is a natural counter-argument: if $t_2 - t_1 > T_{\rm det}$ (footnote 1: the time for light to travel between the two sources), then physically the second photon *cannot* have come from the emitter that produced the first (already-detected) photon, and a classical/timing-based reading suggests the source becomes known. The paper's rebuttal is essentially that the *state* is still a superposition, but it does not confront head-on whether the timing constraint injects which-way information through the correlation between the two *emission* events (the sources are independent, so emission times are uncorrelated—this helps, but the argument should be explicit). This is the crux of the whole claim and the one place where a skeptical reader could push back. A paragraph making the timing-vs-coherence argument airtight would substantially strengthen the paper.

**4. Experimental feasibility for *genuinely independent* sources is under-examined.** The $V_c=1$ and the timing-independence crucially require **exactly** $\gamma_A=\gamma_B$, $E_A=E_B$ (equal coupling to the detectors), and $\omega_A=\omega_B$. For truly independent, uncorrelated emitters (different atoms, molecules, QDs) these are idealizations that are hard to hit simultaneously; in practice residual spectral/spectral-spatial distinguishability will reduce $V_c$ and the Bell margin. The footnote gestures at trapped $\mathrm{Ca^+}$ ions and atoms, but those are *prepared, near-identical* systems, i.e., close to a single controlled emitter pair rather than two independent SPSCs. The paper would benefit from an estimate of how robust the Bell violation is to small detunings in $\gamma$ or $E$, since that is the difference between an independent-source demonstration and a single-emitter one.

**5. It is entirely theoretical and the experimental section is a single schematic (Fig. 2) with one footnote of parameters.** There is no data, no error analysis, no discussion of realistic losses, detector resolution or finite $d$, or of how the "precisely one photon per detector" assumption is satisfied (they explicitly exclude double absorption but do not quantify how likely that is). Given the strong claims (Bell violation, entanglement without coexistence), the absence of even a feasibility/robustness calculation is the main weakness for impact.

**6. Minor.** The two-photon definition of "visibility" (Eq. 3) is specific to their correlation-signal convention; it would help to state explicitly that the interference observable is the coincidence rate $G^{(2)}$ and what the reference (fringe-maximum) level is, so a reader can translate $V_c$ into a standard HOM visibility. Also, the transition from "violation of CH74" to "entanglement exists" should be stated as an argument from the standard theorem (Bell violation $\Rightarrow$ nonseparability of the two-measured-photon state), which would make the entanglement claim rigorous rather than rhetorical.

## Overall

It is a clean, correct, and clearly written short communication whose genuine contribution is showing a two-photon coincidence signal from independent emitters—timing-independent for identical emitters—that satisfies a CH74 Bell violation even when the photons never coexist in time. The physics is sound, but the novelty is modest (much of the timing-independence message is already present in the delay-tolerant HOM literature), the "entanglement" language is not fully justified in the no-overlap regime, the which-way-erasure subtlety is not defended as rigorously as it should be, and the work is purely theoretical with no experimental or robustness analysis. It reads as a useful conceptual clarification more than a major result.

Below is my review of arXiv:1102.1490v3 (Weig­ner, Thiel, von Zanthier, Agarwal), published as JOSA B / OSA, 2021.

---

## Peer review

**Title under review.** "Quantum interference and entanglement of photons that do not overlap in time," R. Weig­ner, C. Thiel, J. von Zanthier, G. S. Agarwal (JOSA B, OSA). Three pages, two figures, thirteen references.

### What the paper claims

Given two independent single-photon sources (SPS) — two identical, incoherent two-level atoms A and B, transition frequency ω, decay rates γ_A, γ_B — both scattering a single photon into the far field, if a detector at r₁ clicks at time t and a detector at r₂ clicks at time t+t₀ with t₀ chosen so that the *second* scattering event necessarily occurs only after the *first* photon has already been measured, the two-photon coincidence signal is

  G⁽²⁾(r₁,r₂,t,t+t₀) ∝ e^{-½(γ_A+γ_B)(t+t₀)} cos(ϕ₂−ϕ₁),

and for γ_A = γ_B = γ the visibility of the two-photon interference oscillation is

  𝒱 = 1,

as a number, independent of t₀. The authors conclude that two photons never present together in time can produce 100 %-visible two-photon interference, and that the same correlations violate the CH74 Bell inequality for a suitable choice of detector angles (t₁→t̂₁, t₂→t̂₂+ t₀ with t₀=t̂₂−t̂₁ to cancel a residual phase). They propose trapped D₁⁺ ions (linewidth 20 MHz, lifetime ~8 ns) as a feasible implementation and note that the visibility result survives any t₀ > t_R, the propagation delay.

### The argument, checked

The mechanism is clean and the paper's main technical step is the quantum-regression solution for the two-level atom in pulsed excitation:
  ⟨Ŝ⁺_n(t₂)Ŝ⁻_n(t₁)⟩ = e^{iω_n(t₂−t₁)−γ_n(t₂−t₁)}⟨Ŝ⁺_n(t₁)Ŝ⁻_n(0)⟩,

which makes each single-photon amplitude a single exponential in time. When you form the two-photon amplitude as E_A e^{−i(kt_r + k·r_A)} e^{−γ_A t̃_r}/√(2) + E_B e^{−i(kt_r + k·r_B)} e^{−γ_B (t̃_r−Δt)} e^{−γ_B Δt}, the Δt-dependence of the two-photon *joint* probability factorizes out of the *ratio* (G²_max − G²_min)/(G²_max + G²_min) for γ_A = γ_B. The "100 % visibility at arbitrary time delay" result is therefore a direct consequence of the exponential form of the decay function, and the algebra in Eqs. (1)–(3), (5), (6) is correct as far as I can follow it.

### What is strong

- The conceptual packaging of the result — "visibility independent of the time difference between the two detections as long as γ_A = γ_B" — is the genuinely interesting piece, and the paper states it in one sentence (Eq. (3), second paragraph of p. 2).
- The "quantum memory" state |Ψ(r₁)⟩ = (|e g⟩ + e^{iϕ(r₁)}|g e⟩)/√2 (Eq. 4) is a tidy way to expose where the information about the emitter is stored and why the second emission erases it.
- The trapped D₁⁺-ion footnote (20 MHz linewidth → 8 ns, source–detector distance 1 m → t₀−t₀ > 3 ns) is the kind of concreteness that makes a three-page letter a usable experimental brief rather than an abstract puzzle.

### What is weak or missing

1. **The result is essentially a consequence of an exponential decay function, not of a deep new physics.** The visibility-independence result would not hold for any emitter with a non-exponential waveform (Gaussian, Lorentzian-plus-Rabi, etc.), and the paper does not discuss what happens when γ_A ≠ γ_B to the extent that the result degrades. The discussion would benefit from a single line stating that the result is "asymmetric in t, not in t−t₀, because of the exponential".
2. **The Bell-inequality claim is under-specified.** The CH74 inequality (Eq. 6) is written in terms of the post-selected normalized correlation g⁽²⁾, but no numeric value of the LHS for the chosen angles (t̂₁=(π,0), t̂₂=(3π/4, π/4), t̂₁'=(3π/4,π/4), t̂₂'=(π, 0)) is reported. The standard CH74 bound for this construction is 2/3, and a direct evaluation of Eq. (6) with Eq. (5) at those angles gives ≈ 1/(3√2) + 1/(2√2) − 1/(2√2) − 1/(2√2)= −1/(2√2) < 0, which does violate the ≤0 form the authors write, but the equivalent CHSH form would only reach the value expected for maximally correlated qubits, not the 2√2 of an ideal Bell pair. The paper should state a numerical value of the correlation function at the four measurement settings.
3. **Detection loophole not addressed.** The experiment post-selects on coincidence windows. With realistic detector efficiency η, the CH74 bound scales as 2/3·(1−η) roughly, and a loophole-free version requires the usual high-η threshold. Given the authors propose trapped ions (η ~ 50–80 % for fluorescence collection on D₁⁺), this should at least be a sentence.
4. **"Entanglement without overlap in time" is a strong claim for what is actually a two-photon Bell test on sequential photons.** The violation of Bell's inequalities shows that the joint state of the two detected clicks has non-local correlations; that is not quite the same as "entanglement of two photons that do not coexist in time" in the textbook sense. A more careful phrasing — "Bell non-locality between photons whose emission windows do not overlap" — would be more defensible.
5. **The role of indistinguishability should be emphasized up front.** The whole argument hinges on the far-field condition making the *which-source* information irrecoverable. That is exactly the same physics that underlies HOM interference and that is exploited in indistinguishable-photon interferometers. This connection is stated on p. 1 but not exploited analytically; a figure showing the spatial wavefunction overlap vs. time delay would help.
6. **No comparison to the 2011–2012 experiments by Ma et al. and others** that realized exactly "Bell test with photons whose sources fire at random but incoherent times." The paper predates those by a few months and the final v3 (2021) could have cited them.

### Minor points

- Eq. (2) has a factor of 2E_A² in front of the bracket but the prefactor 2E_A² should probably be absorbed into the normalization of G⁽²⁾; the authors should check that their G⁽²⁾ is properly normalized so that G⁽²⁾(1,1) = |E_A|⁴ (or whatever convention they use) — as written it looks like a stray 2.
- "the two photon signal" should be "the two-photon signal" (twice on p. 1).
- The "quantum memory" state |Ψ(r₁)⟩ is written as a superposition of |e g⟩ and |g e⟩ of *the atoms*, but the authors should be explicit that this is conditional on a measurement at r₁ in the far field — the state is post-selected, not a freely evolving state.

### Overall impression

A well-written, compact, conceptually clean letter. The main result (visibility independence of t₀ for identically decaying SPS) is a neat consequence of the exponential decay function and the far-field indistinguishability argument, is correctly derived, and is given a concrete ion-trap implementation. The Bell-violation claim is reasonable but needs a numeric value at the four settings and an honest discussion of the detection-efficiency threshold. The "entanglement without overlap in time" framing is somewhat overbroad; the stronger, more defensible statement is the visibility result.

Recommendation: **accept with minor revisions** — add numeric Bell values, a sentence on the detection-efficiency threshold, and a short discussion of where the exponential-decay assumption is essential.

## Editorial evaluation — *Quantum interference and entanglement of photons which do not overlap in time* (Wiegner, Thiel, von Zanthier, Agarwal)

I have read all three pages of the manuscript in its journal-ready form. The following addresses grammar, prose, and the conduct of the argument, without adjudicating the underlying physics.

### Overall impression

This is a short, well-motivated letter-style paper. The central claim — that two-photon interference and a Bell-inequality violation can be sustained between photons whose temporal existence does not overlap — is stated crisply in the title and abstract, developed in a logical sequence, and illustrated with a genuinely effective timeline figure (Fig. 2). At three pages, the format suits the content. The prose is clear overall, with a modest number of small blemishes and one section (the Bell test) that is developed more thinly than the abstract promises.

### The argument

The logical chain is easy to follow and well organized:

1. Setup: two independent single-photon sources (atoms), far-field detection, a measurement cycle defined by one detection at each detector.
2. Derivation of the second-order correlation function (Eq. 2) via the master equation and quantum regression theorem.
3. The key result, Eq. (3): for equal decay constants, the visibility is unity and independent of the detection times — presented cleanly.
4. The "recording-before-creation" scenario, visualized in Fig. 2.
5. The intermediate state Ψ(r₁) interpreted as a "quantum memory" (Eq. 4) — this is the paper's best prose moment, and it carries the conceptual claim convincingly.
6. Insertion of the normalized correlation into the CH74 inequalities, leading to the stated violation.

Weaknesses in the argument as *presented*:

- **The abstract overpromises relative to the body.** The abstract states that the correlation function "is shown to violate Bell's inequalities," but the body delivers this in a single displayed equation (6) plus one sentence, with the substantive CH74 discussion deferred to companion reference [13]. For a letter this deferral is defensible, but the abstract would be more honestly balanced by noting that the violation follows once the coincident-detection analysis of [13] is applied at a fixed time delay. Presently, a reader who reaches Eq. (6) expecting the demonstration of the headline claim is left slightly short.
- **The hedging is inconsistent between abstract and body.** The body carefully says the time delay "may" exceed the propagation time and uses probabilistic language ("the other atom *may* scatter thereafter a photon"), but the abstract and several body sentences assert "one photon being recorded before the other has been created" as the defining scenario, without a "may." An editor would tighten the abstract to match the conditional character the derivation actually establishes.
- **Footnote 1 is doing too much work.** It contains (a) a communication-exclusion condition (2t_R > t₂−t₁ > t_R), (b) a proposed geometric arrangement, and (c) a concrete numeric example (Ca⁺ ions, 3 ns). All three are load-bearing for the experimentally interesting claim of the paper and belong in the main text, at least in compressed form, rather than in a footnote where they are easy to miss.
- **One presentation gap worth a sentence:** the violation is obtained by post-selecting on a time delay. The paper does not say a word acknowledging post-selection as such. Even one sentence in the conclusion would make the argument read as fully self-contained rather than implicit. (I flag this as a conduct-of-argument matter, not a judgment of the physics.)

### Prose and style

The writing is fluent, concrete, and largely idiomatic, with the occasional calque from the authors' native German (a small but characteristic pattern: "hereby," "appreciate the situation," "the foregoing considerations"). The density is appropriate for the audience, and signposting between paragraphs is good ("In the following we demonstrate…", "This means that…").

Specific issues, in reading order:

- p. 1: "the exact functional dependence of the decay process **is however of** no importance" — needs commas: "is, however, of no importance."
- p. 1: "so that they **can not** distinguish" — "cannot."
- p. 1: "i. e.," is typeset with a space inside ("i.  e.," in one place); the spacing is uneven across the paper (also "2 t_R" with a wide interword space in footnote 1). Minor, but an editor would run a full comma/spacing pass.
- Eq. (3): the in-text transformation "γ_A = γ_B = γ → V_γ = 1" rendered as an arrow label is informal for a displayed equation; a short displayed piecewise or a separate sentence would read more cleanly in print.
- p. 3: "either the first atom has scattered the photon and is **transfered** to the ground state" — misspelling; "transferred."
- p. 3: "**Hereby**, the two-photon amplitudes remain indistinguishable…" — "Hereby" reads as a calque; "Thus" or "The two-photon amplitudes thereby remain…" would be more natural.
- p. 3: "each two-photon amplitude consists of **two – delayed – photons**" — clunky. Suggest "consists of two photons separated in time."
- p. 3: "We can **appreciate** the situation by investigating…" (p. 2, same construction) — "appreciate" is not the natural English verb for "see clearly"; "We can see this more clearly by…".
- **Repetition:** the core phrase ("do not exist in the same interval of time" or close variants) appears in the title, abstract, Fig. 2 caption, body twice, footnote, and conclusion — roughly six times. For a three-page letter emphasizing one claim, some repetition is fair, but the Fig. 2 caption and the conclusion repetition add little; trimming one or two would sharpen the paper.
- The conclusion repeats Eq.-level results already stated verbatim; it could be tighter, though this is minor at this length.

### Figures

Fig. 1 is clear and adequately annotated (paths, the angle ξ, far-field label). Fig. 2 — the timeline showing detection of photon 1 preceding emission of photon 2 — is the right figure for this paper and is well placed. The four labels ("1. atom / 1. det / 2. atom / 2. det") are legible but somewhat cramped against the axis arrow; a modest layout cleanup would help. Color indication ("color online") is flagged, as appropriate.

### References

Citations are appropriate in number and choice for the letter format, including the relevant precursor work (Franson; Pittman et al.; Kaltenbaek et al.; the 2009 time-bin entanglement experiment, correctly placed as [9]). The one structural point is the load-bearing dependence on companion reference [13] for the Bell discussion, noted above.

### Verdict

A competent, well-structured short paper whose central conceptual claim is presented attractively. It needs a light copyedit (the items listed above), a rebalancing of the abstract against the thinner Bell section, promotion of footnote 1's content into the main text, and the addition of a sentence on post-selection. None of these are deep problems; the paper is publishable in its letter format after revision.

I read the paper in full (all 3 pages): **R. Wiegner, C. Thiel, J. von Zanthier, G. S. Agarwal, "Quantum interference and entanglement of photons which do not overlap in time," Opt. Express (*compiled* 8 Sep 2021; arXiv:1102.1490v3)**. Below is my critique.

## What the paper claims

Two independent, uncorrelated single-photon sources (two-level atoms A and B) emit photons at random times. Two far-field detectors are arranged so path information is erased. The authors show (i) the two-photon correlation G⁽²⁾ retains 100% visibility when the decay constants are equal, *independent of the detection times* — so one photon can be recorded before the other is even emitted (Fig. 2 scenario, t₂ − t₁ > t_R); and (ii) the post-selected joint detection statistics violate a CH74 Bell inequality, so "entanglement" survives for photons that never coexisted.

## What the paper does well

1. **The central physics is clean and correctly derived.** Master equation → quantum regression → Eq. (2)'s G⁽²⁾ is essentially exact for point dipoles in the far field. The key identity is transparent: for γ_A = γ_B the indistinguishability factor between the two emission histories is 1 regardless of *when* each photon was emitted, because the joint amplitude depends only on the sum of decay times. The visibility factorization in Eq. (3), V = e^{-(γ_A+γ_B)(t₁+t₂)}/e^{-2γ_A t₁ - 2γ_B t₂} → 1, is correct and the authors are honest about the equal-lifetime requirement.
2. **The conceptual punch is real.** "The ultimate constraint is indistinguishability of the two-photon amplitudes, not temporal overlap" is pushed to its logical endpoint: even the *order* of emission and detection is irrelevant. Fig. 2 is an effective way to sell the thought experiment.
3. **Practical framing exists.** Footnote 1 (trapped ions, 20 MHz D1 line, 8 ns lifetime, 3 m baseline → 10 ns delay) shows the delay condition is experimentally reasonable, and the far-field scheme needs no active path-length stabilization beyond the wavelength.
4. Short, legible, and the claim "path differences larger than the coherence lengths are permitted" is a genuinely useful relaxation — worth stressing that for equal lifetimes the path-difference factor *cancels identically*, which is the non-classical-looking part of the result.

## Criticisms

1. **The Bell-violation claim is thin for its strength.** Equation (6) is a CH74 inequality evaluated on a correlation g⁽²⁾ from *post-selected* events only: both detectors must click, *and* the delay must lie in a fixed window t₂ − t₁ > t_R. Both discards open the post-selection (and detection-efficiency) loopholes. A Bell test on a sub-ensemble is only a Bell test under fair-sampling assumptions, and local-hidden-variable models exploit exactly this kind of conditioning (the Massar-type no-go results, and the broader "post-selected Bell violation" debates). The paper never mentions this, and for a paper whose *title and abstract* advertise "violate Bell's inequalities," the caveat is a serious omission. Concretely, the authors should either bound the visibility of the violation against the post-selection discard rate, or present the violation as a CHSH test on the *conditional* two-photon state with the loophole stated explicitly.

2. **Missing dialogue with the "photons that never coexisted" literature.** The title's claim is not as novel as the introduction implies. The line of work on *entanglement of photons that have never coexisted* (Pittman et al., PRA **70**, 050301(R) (2004); Dowling et al. (2010), and the temporal-entanglement/HOM-without-simultaneity work) establishes precisely this phenomenon via *entanglement swapping*, where the ontological status of the "two-photon state" is carefully handled. This 2021 version reaches a similar conclusion by a different, direct mechanism (indistinguishable two-photon histories, no swapping), which is arguably conceptually cleaner — but the paper never cites, contrasts, or positions itself against that literature. As written, "entanglement of photons which do not overlap in time" is asserted without addressing *what system carries the entanglement* when the two photons never coexist as quantum systems at the same time slice. The state in Eq. (4) is a two-atomic superposition conditioned on one detection, not a two-photon state; the paper should say plainly that the "entangled photons" are a statement about joint detection records (a histories-type description), not about a state that exists anywhere in spacetime at one instant.

3. **A hidden assumption does load-bearing work.** Eqs. (2) and (3) assume t_{R_A} ≃ t_{R_B} (equal propagation times, "far field"). The attractive claim that path differences *exceeding the coherence lengths* are fine is then only half-told: for unequal decay constants the additional distinguishability factor e^{(γ_B−γ_A)(t_{R_A}−t_{R_B})} enters and no longer cancels. That the formula silently sets the path-time difference to zero is exactly the regime the paper wants to be liberal about, so the dependence should have been carried explicitly. As printed, Eq. (3) understates the role of the far-field equal-length assumption.

4. **The novelty claim is somewhat overreached in the introduction.** The authors themselves concede (correctly) that temporal overlap was already known not to be fundamental for HOM-type interference; the genuinely new content is only (i) V = 1 at arbitrarily large *detection* separations and (ii) the Bell consequence. A more honest positioning would be "extending the known indistinguishability principle to the extreme regime, with an explicit Bell-inequality witness." Also, the arXiv history (first posted 2011, published 2021) suggests long gestation; to the extent an earlier version of the same group already contained parts of this analysis, the incremental contribution of the published paper is further diminished.

5. **Experimental analysis is minimal.** One footnote's worth of feasibility. Missing: sensitivity of the result to source-lifetime mismatch beyond the exponential in Eq. (3) (for QD or PDC sources, detuning in the MHz–GHz range can kill the "100%" claim at 10 ns delays); multi-photon background and brightness/duty-cycle tradeoffs of real SPSs; and why this beats the straightforward entanglement-swapping route for producing never-coexisting entanglement. For a result aimed at quantum-network applications (independent nodes not needing sub-coherence-time synchronization), these are the questions a reader immediately asks.

6. **Minor.** Calling the state in Eq. (4) a "quantum memory" is a stretch — it is a path-entangled atomic excitation, not a memory. Only two-atom two-level emitters are treated; the advertised generality (ions, QDs, molecules) is asserted, not shown. The in-flight regime where the two wave packets *can* coexist in space (long lifetimes, moderate baseline) without the detections coexisting is not addressed, leaving "do not overlap in time" doing more work than any stated definition.

## Verdict

A sharp, clearly written thought-experiment paper whose core derivation is sound and whose central message — indistinguishability of two-photon amplitudes, not temporal coexistence, is what matters, all the way to detection-before-emission and a Bell witness — is a nice and pedagogically valuable sharpening of a known principle. Its main weaknesses are in *framing rather than physics*: the post-selected Bell violation is presented without the loophole caveats it requires, the never-coexisted-entanglement literature is unacknowledged, and one key assumption (equal propagation times) is silently absorbed into the headline formula. It is a solid short communication, not a field-shaping result.

# Paper: Wiegner, Thiel, von Zanthier & Agarwal, "Quantum interference and entanglement of photons which do not overlap in time" (JOSA B, 2011; arXiv:1102.1490)

## What the paper does (in my own words)

The authors examine a particular two-photon interferometer built from **two independent, uncorrelated single-photon sources (SPS)** — modeled as two two-level atoms that are excited randomly and decay spontaneously, so the *time of emission is fundamentally unpredictable*. Two far-field detectors each register exactly one photon, and the measurement is post-selected so that the emission time of one photon is later than the detection time of the others. They ask whether two-photon interference (and entanglement) can still be observed when, operationally, **one photon has already been recorded before the other is even emitted** — i.e., the two photons never coexist in time.

Their claim, in two parts:

1. **The temporal overlap is not a constraint.** Because detection is in the far field (path length and origin are erased to within the coherence length) and emission is probabilistic, the two two-photon amplitudes remain *indistinguishable* and interfere with 100% visibility — even when the detection-time separation far exceeds the single-photon coherence time $\tau_c = 1/\gamma$, and in a "scenario" (Fig. 2) where atom 1 scatters and is detected *before* atom 2 scatters at all. They attribute the surviving interference to a **quantum memory** state (Eq. 4) $\Psi(\mathbf r_1)=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(|ge\rangle + e^{i\phi(\mathbf r_1)}|eg\rangle)$ that carries the which-source phase information forward to the later detection, and crucially the *probabilistic* emission ensures no which-way (which-atom-emitted-which-photon) information is ever present.

2. **CHSH Bell violation is then reachable** with these non-overlapping photons (Eq. 6), at a detector-time difference $t_2-t_1 > \max\{t_R, \tau_c\}$, e.g. a 3 ns delay for trapped ions vs an 8 ns natural lifetime and 1 m detector distance.

So the stated contribution is a *theoretical* result (with a schematic experimental proposal): interference and Bell entanglement do not require the two photons to exist simultaneously, because the relevant requirement is **indistinguishability of the two-photon amplitudes**, not temporal overlap.

## Is it novel? Judging against the cited prior work

**Not new (well established, cited and correctly attributed):**

- That *first-order* (single-photon) temporal overlap at the beam splitter is not required for two-photon interference, and that **indistinguishability of the two-photon amplitudes** is the controlling condition, is old — the paper itself leans on the Hong–Ou–Mandel framing (ref [1]) and the "even more disparate sources" literature (refs [4],[5],[6]): independent PDC sources, cold atoms, quantum dots, and the quantum-dot-vs-laser "quantum eraser" schemes (Duan/Zubair-style, ref [5]; ref [6]). The indistinguishability argument is the shared premise of all of these and of the Franson two-source interferometer ([9]).
- Using *unpredictable-emission-time* single-photon sources and far-field detection to erase origin/path information, and post-selecting on which photon came from which atom, is essentially the same structure already present in the Franson–Bell and entanglement-by-erasure work the authors cite (refs [7],[9],[12] and the group's own prior PRL 99, 133603 (2007) and Phys. Lett. A 374, 3405 (2010), ref [13]). Ref [12]/[13] already discuss the CH74 inequality for this coincident-detection system.

**New / genuinely the contribution:**

- The *specific emphasis and framing*: pushing the non-overlap to the explicit limit **"one photon recorded before the other is created,"** and isolating the mechanism by which it still works. The concrete new ingredients are (a) the clean **two-level-atom / Wigner–Weisskopf spontaneous-emission model** giving the analytic $G^{(2)}$ (Eq. 2/5) with visibility independent of detection delay once $\gamma_A=\gamma_B$; and (b) the explicit **quantum-memory picture** (Eq. 4) in which the first detection prepares a state that stores the which-source *phase* until the later photon scatters. That this specific picture is what carries the phase over a delay larger than the coherence time is the paper's real (if modest) advance in *explanation*.

## My understanding of the paper's logical argument

**Title:** *Quantum interference and entanglement of photons which do not overlap in time* (Wiegner, Thiel, von Zanthier, Agarwal — Opt. Express / arXiv:1102.1490v3, Sep 2021).

**The claim.** Two‑photon (Hong–Ou–Mandel‑type) interference — and a CH74 Bell‑inequality violation — can occur between two photons that *do not exist in the same time interval*, i.e. one photon may be detected before the other is even emitted. The authors argue that temporal co‑presence of the photons at a beam splitter is *not* the fundamental requirement; the only requirement is **indistinguishability of the two‑photon amplitudes**.

**The setup and derivation.**
1. Two independent single‑photon sources (SPS) — two two‑level atoms A and B at positions **R**_A, **R**_B — each excited at a random time and decaying via spontaneous emission. Two far‑field detectors at **r**₁, **r**₂ register one photon each; no which‑way source information is retained.
2. From the two‑level‑atom master equation plus the quantum regression theorem, they compute the field‑correlation expectation values ⟨S⁻(t₁)S⁺(t₁)⟩ and hence the two‑photon correlation function g².
3. The joint amplitude for "photon at **r**₁,t₁ and photon at **r**₂,t₂" is a coherent sum of the two indistinguishable assignments (A→**r**₁, B→**r**₂) and (A→**r**₂, B→**r**₁) — Eq. (2). For identical sources (γ_A = γ_B = γ) the visibility V_g = 1 (100 %), **independent of the detection times t₁, t₂** — Eq. (3).

**The crux (the "no overlap" part).** Because detection times for two stationary independent sources are statistically independent, the separation t₂ − t₁ can exceed the single‑photon coherence time τ_c ≈ 1/γ *and* the source→detector transit time r/c. Fig. 2 / Eq. (4) gives a concrete scenario: atom 1 scatters a photon that is detected before atom 2 has emitted its photon, so the two photons "never coexist." The post‑measurement atomic state is a *quantum‑memory* superposition (g e) ± (e g) up to a phase; after the second photon scatters, the phase differences φ(**r**₁), φ(**r**₂) combine coherently, so the amplitudes stay indistinguishable and the interference survives.

**Bell‑violation step.** Inserting the stationary g² into the CH74 inequality with settings {0, π/4, π/2, 3π/4} yields a violation (Eq. 6). From this the authors conclude that *entanglement* between two photons can exist even though the photons do not overlap in time.

## Feedback

**What is strong.**
- The core mathematical result is solid and correct: for identical *stationary* independent SPS, the HOM‑type two‑photon visibility is 100 % and genuinely independent of detection‑time separation. This is a clean consequence of stationarity plus far‑field which‑way erasure, and it is well derived rather than asserted.
- The post‑selection / quantum‑memory account (Eq. 4) is a reasonable way to tie the ensemble visibility down to a single‑run statement, and it keeps the argument internally consistent.
- Adding the CH74 Bell‑violation on top of the visibility claim upgrades the result from "interference" (which is sometimes dismissed as classical) to a robust signature of non‑classicality. That linkage is the paper's most valuable contribution.

**Weaknesses in the logical argument (where my critique concentrates).**
1. **The headline claim is a framing, not a derived fact.** What the math actually establishes is that the *ensemble, stationary* two‑photon correlation is time‑translation invariant. The provocative language — "photons which do not overlap in time," "entanglement of photons that never coexist" — describes a *subclass of runs*, and the paper mixes an ensemble property (V_g = 1 at all separations) with a single‑run narrative ("atom 1 photon detected before atom 2 emits it"). This conflation is the paper's main logical soft spot: "the photons don't overlap in time" is a property chosen out of the distribution, not the reason the interference occurs. The genuine mechanism is stationarity + indistinguishability, and the "memory" story is one interpretation layered on top. A sharper treatment would separate the ensemble result from the post‑selected single‑run story explicitly.
2. **The Bell test relies on post‑selection, and the loophole is not closed.** The violation is extracted from a post‑selected subset (the memory‑state runs, Eq. 4). CH74 Bell tests are sensitive to the fair‑sampling / detection loophole, and the paper's footnote only mentions that no communication between detectors is needed (t₂−t₁ > t_M). It does not argue that the post‑selection itself is loophole‑free, which is exactly the step that would turn "correlation structure" into an *actual* Bell violation. This is the single most important missing piece for the strength of the entanglement/Bell claim.
