## Editorial review — *Reflected light from giant planets in habitable zones: Tapping into the power of the Cross-Correlation Function*

I've read the full 10-page article (text, figures, tables, references). Below I assess it as an editor: grammar, style, prose, and the coherence of the argument — deliberately setting aside the scientific merit.

### Overall impression

This is a competent, readable, and well-organized feasibility paper written in careful but plainly non-native English. The argument has a clean and logical shape: (1) the obstacle is the tiny planet-to-star flux ratio; (2) the Cross-Correlation Function (CCF) boosts the minute planetary signal and has already succeeded on 51 Pegasi b; (3) apply the same logic to giant planets in their hosts' habitable zones, using ESO's E-ELT exposure-time calculator; (4) report integration times, with five targets coming in under 100 h. Each section follows predictably from the last, the figures and tables are well placed, and the discussion returns neatly to the opening problem. An editor would **green-light the structure and logic** but would order a **thorough copyedit before publication**, because the prose carries a steady stream of small grammatical errors.

### Grammar (recurring, specific errors)

There is a cluster of the same kind of mistakes — wrong prepositions, a recurring "allow to" construction, and subject–verb agreement slips — that a native editor would flag on almost every page:

- **Subject/verb split by a comma** — "Transmission spectroscopy (e.g. Charbonneau et al. 2002, Knutson et al. 2014), *relies* on the filtering…" (p. 1). The comma wrongly separates the subject from its verb.
- **Compound subject + singular verb** — "Occultation photometry and spectroscopy *measures* the wavelength dependency…" (p. 1).
- **"allow to" (appears more than once)** — "the measurement of the flux variation of a planet allows to reconstruct the planetary phase variation" (p. 1); and in §4 "this technique … *should allow to achieve* the SN level required…" (p. 8). *Allow* cannot take a bare infinitive here; "allow *us* to…" or "make it possible to…" is needed.
- **Wrong preposition** — "an increase **on** S/N by a factor of ~65" (p. 2) → *in*.
- **"the same … of"** — "we adopted the same criteria **of** the Habitable Exoplanet Catalog" (p. 3) → *as those of / as*.
- **Missing preposition** — "Please note that **this analysis we assume** that the FWHM…" (p. 7) → *in this analysis*.
- **Dropped noun** — "a high rotation rate of the planet will cause **the reflected** to be broadened" (p. 7) → *the reflected signal*.
- **Missing possessive** — "as seen from **the planet rest frame**" (p. 7).
- **Extra article / broken parallelism** — "the cases of Gliese876 c and **the** HIP57050 b" (p. 8).
- **"equals to"** — "yielding a SN for a 3-sigma detection **equals to** 1.5 × 10⁵" (p. 8) → *equal to/… of*.
- **Agreement** — "a degree of complexity that **rival** our own Solar System" (p. 1) → *rivals*.

There are also typographical slips — "30s", "100h", "2 ×10⁻⁷" (spacing), the non-word **"unabroadened"** (p. 7), "mag*", and inconsistent hyphenation ("planet-to star" vs "planet-to-star", "next generation" vs "next-generation", "hot-Jupiters" vs "hot Jupiter").

### Style and tone

The prose is a little over-hyped in places for a technical article: "we propose to **unleash the power** of the Cross Correlation Function" (abstract), "**Tapping into the power** of the Cross-Correlation Function" (title), "a **powerful ally** to the detection of the minute reflected optical signal," and "make it surface above the noise level." These would read more convincingly if trimmed. The name of the method itself is spelled inconsistently — "Cross Correlation Function" and "Cross‑Correlation Function" both appear. There is one noticeably clunky run-on sentence about satellite systems (final paragraph of §4) that would benefit from being split.

### Argumentation

For a feasibility study the argument is **clear and self-consistent**, and the caveats are handled well (the 25 % assumed E-ELT efficiency is explicitly flagged as indicative; the CCF-FWHM assumption is called out; the non-habitable-giant-with-habitable-satellite angle is honestly qualified). The main weakness on the argument side is modest scope and a degree of circularity — the approach simply re-applies the Martins et al. 2013/2015 CCF result to a new sample of targets and reports observing times, so the paper is more an application/extrapolation than a methodological advance. A reader wanting a stronger "so what" might want the five sub-100 h targets treated with a bit more detail on what a detection would actually yield.

### References

The reference list is generally consistent (alphabetical, year-styled, with DOIs), but a few entries show character-encoding corruption — e.g. "DASó©opyrightgransan" in the May et al. 2011 author line and "Leikeird" in Knutson et al. 2014 — which needs to be cleaned up before press.

### Verdict

Publish-able as a solid, well-argued **feasibility/observing proposal**, contingent on a full language edit to remove the recurring preposition/agreement/"allow to" errors, a light pass on the more florid phrasing, and a fix of the corrupted reference entries. The writing never genuinely obscures the argument, which is the key editorial test for a non-specialist reviewer.

On the review rubric (weighing originality of approach and field impact lightly on science, per the brief, and judging overall quality with emphasis on the argument and presentation): the *idea* is an incremental extension of a published method to a new target population (moderate originality); the *paper itself* is coherent, readable, and well structured but limited in scope and marked by a clear but fixable set of language errors (decent overall); and its *impact* is that of one useful contribution toward next-generation facility planning rather than a field-shaping result (modest impact).

# Critique of "Reflected light from giant planets in habitable zones: Tapping into the power of the Cross-Correlation Function" (Martins et al., arXiv:1604.01086v1)

## Overview

This is a short feasibility study (8 pages + references) that projects whether the Cross Correlation Function (CCF) technique — successfully applied by the same group to the hot-Jupiter 51 Pegasi b (Martins et al. 2015) — could recover the *reflected* (day-side, optical) spectral signatures of **giant planets in the habitable zones (HZ)** of their host stars using the E-ELT (39 m). For 34 HZ giant planets (K/M dwarfs, $F<10$, $T_{\rm eff}=2000$–$8000$ K), the authors compute the maximum planet-to-star flux ratio, feed it into ESO's Exposure Time Calculator, and scale up the required integration time for a 3-$\sigma$ detection. Their headline result: **5 targets need less than ~100 hours**, and even current 10-m class telescopes could reach < 40 h for the two closest (Gliese 876 b/c, HIP 57050 b).

## What the paper does well

1. **Clear, self-contained framing.** The problem (optical planet/star ratio $\sim10^{-8}$), the technique (CCF amplifies by $\sqrt{N_{\rm lines}}$, $\sim$65 for HARPS), and the scaling to the E-ELT are all explained simply. Equation 1 gives the standard reflected-light phase-integral estimate.
2. **An honest catalogue-based approach.** Rather than cherry-picking a single best target, they build a reproducible sample from the exoplanet.eu database using the Habitable Exoplanet Catalog HZ model, which makes the claim testable.
3. **The central physical point is fair.** That HZ planets around M dwarfs — despite faint hosts — can be *brighter in reflected starlight* than HZ planets around bright $F$-type stars is a genuinely useful and non-obvious observation (the HZ hugs bright stars, so $a$ is small and the ratio scales $\sim 1/a^2$).

## Major weaknesses

**1. The single dominant assumption is unvalidated for this case: the CCF gain scales with $\sqrt{N_{\rm lines}}$ and the planet's CCF has the star's FWHM.** The whole feasibility claim rides on extrapolating the 51 Peg *hot-Jupiter* CCF SN gain out to HZ giant planets, but:

- **HZ planets are far more distant and tidally locked (or near-circumstellar) in a *very* different way.** The 51 Peg success relied on a large, phase-varying, *moving* signal with a known orbital velocity amplitude. HZ giant planets on $\sim60$–$1000$-day orbits have tiny radial velocities; extracting a CCF that shifts by only a few km/s against the stellar lines requires extremely precise stellar subtraction and *phase-folding to a period of order 1 yr*, which is not what CCF does in the standard Doppler sense. The paper never addresses how the planetary CCF is isolated from the star when the orbital velocity is this small — star-removal (the dotted line in their own Figure 1) becomes dramatically harder, and this is precisely where the $\sqrt{N}$ gain degrades to a *noise floor* dominated by residual telluric/stellar systematic noise.
- **The assumption that the planet's CCF FWHM equals the star's** is flagged once in passing (§3) but is actually a *serious* issue. A cool HZ giant reflects a *reprocessed* stellar spectrum; its "mask lines" are not the star's absorption lines — the planet's reflected light carries the *stellar* spectrum, not a planetary absorption template, so the very *mask* used in CCF is questionable (a reflected signal is a *scaled, shifted copy of the star*, not the planetary atmospheric CCF). The 51 Peg 2015 result used *reflected* light but the CCF mask was stellar. The paper does not discuss mask construction, which is load-bearing.

**2. Integration time is dominated by *systematics*, not photon noise.** Equation 5–6 scale a 30-second ETC SN purely by flux ($-5\log$ SN ratio between magnitudes), then by $1/N_{\rm lines}^{-2}$. This is a **photon-shot-noise-limited** estimate. For a $\sim10^{-7}$ signal at R=100,000, the realistic floor is speckle/instrument/systematic noise at $\sim10^{-5}$–$10^{-6}$ per resolution element (cf. high-resolution direct-imaging work — e.g., the "systematic noise floor" documented in the 51 Peg and HR 8799 HRC work). Without an explicit systematic-noise floor, the <100 h numbers for the 5 closest targets are, at best, optimistic by factors of ~10–100. The paper treats the ETC as if it could be stacked to arbitrary depth.

**3. The "5 planets, <100 h" result is not robust to the stated albedo uncertainty.** Table 1 uses $A_g=0.3$ for *all* unknowns. For cold HZ giant planets the actual geometric albedo is poorly known and *likely lower* (no strong Rayleigh/cloudy day-side in the same way as hot Jupiters), and the *phase curve* at opposition for a cold planet is a small crescent (phase function $g(\alpha)$ is far from unity). The factor of several the authors note is actually much larger, and could move all 5 "easy" targets to >1000 h. The albedo is the *weakest* link and it is treated as a fixed assumption.

**4. Sample selection quietly biases toward the easy cases.** Restricting to $F<10$, $T_{\rm eff}$ in 2000–8000 K, and HZ with the Kasting/Whitemire/Reynolds 1993 model (not the more conservative Kopparapu 2013), and using the *empirical* radius-mass-flux relation (Eq. 3) rather than measured radii where available, means the "5 easy" set could be substantially smaller (or the HZ definitions alone could shift which planets qualify) with a different HZ model. There is no sensitivity analysis across HZ definitions, no error bars on the exposure times, and no statement of the *fraction* of the total known sample that is reachable — the honest statistic is "5 out of 34 HZ giants" ≈ 15%.

**5. No comparison to competing or concurrent techniques.** In 2016, high-contrast imaging (SPHERE, Gemini/GPI) at longer wavelengths and future interferometric/mid-IR facilities (JWST, ELT/Metis) are natural benchmarks. The paper is written in a vacuum; it never asks "is the E-ELT CCF the best route, or is there a better one?" This is a weakness for a feasibility study, because the *point* of such a paper is to justify the investment.

**6. Writing and presentation.** 
- Table 1's "5.6 × 10^4" flux ratio column and "1.9 × 10^3" are clearly **flux ratio × 10⁻⁸** and should be labelled; the "×10⁻⁸" is buried in the table caption. 
- Figure 4's y-axis is logarithmic (10⁻¹ up to 5000 h) with a dense wall of ~5000 h bars and a couple of short green bars; it is hard to read the actual numbers. Table 4 provides the readable version.
- The claim "SN for 3-sigma detection equals to $1.5\times10^{-7}$" in the Discussion is confused — that is the *flux ratio*, not the SN.
- Figure 2 (the recovered 51 Peg CCF) is re-used verbatim from Martins et al. 2015 without re-plotting or stating exactly which of those figures it is; the red line is the fit model but this is not labelled in the caption.
- The conclusion is mildly over-claimed: "yields them good prospects towards the detection of a habitable planet similar to our own" — the targets are *giants*, and a giant in the HZ is not a habitable planet in the strict sense; the authors note satellites in a footnote but then blur the distinction in the conclusion.

## Minor / technical points

- The HZ constants from Selsis et al. 2007 / Underwood, Jones & Sleep 2003 with $T_s$=5700 K are used for *all* stars in the $r_i, r_o$ formulae — this is a standard shortcut but worth stating that the HZ width will shift noticeably for $M_3$ (55 Cnc) vs. M4V vs. F-type hosts.
- Eq. 5 uses a 5-mag SN relation appropriate only in the *photon-noise* regime; at R=100,000 the SN per pixel on the blue side of M dwarfs can be sky/flat-field limited, which the authors acknowledge only implicitly.
- The 25% ETC efficiency is the *total* system throughput; the CCF gain of ~89 (from $\sqrt{4100}$ HARPS lines) does *not* automatically transfer to a 100,000-line E-ELT/HIRES-class mask in the optical if the SN per line is below unity — there is a crossover the authors don't discuss.
- The "1.9 R_⊞" radius for 51 Peg b and other figures are cited to Martins et al. 2015 but the *independent* check against Brogi et al. 2013 is only a consistency check of the *mass*; the radius is assumed.
- No numerical simulations / mock-CCF pipeline is presented. For a feasibility claim of this kind, an end-to-end Monte Carlo (draw a realistic stellar + planet + telluric spectrum, run the real CCF pipeline, compute the recovered SN, repeat at multiple S/N) would be far more persuasive than the analytic ETC scaling.

## Bottom line

This is a reasonable *first-order* feasibility sketch, clearly written, with a real and interesting physical insight (M-dwarf HZ giants can be the easiest HZ reflected-light targets). But its central quantitative result (5 planets reachable in <100 h on the E-ELT; <40 h on VLT-class) rests on three untested and likely-over-optimistic assumptions: (a) the CCF $\sqrt{N}$ SN scaling extends to tiny-amplitude, near-locked HZ planetary signals; (b) photon noise — not the systematic-noise floor of high-resolution stellar differential spectroscopy — sets the detection limit; and (c) unknown-albedo HZ giants retain geometric albedos of order 0.3. None of these is tested with a simulation. The 5/34 success rate, and its sensitivity to HZ definition, albedo, and phase-function, are understated. As submitted, this is a **plausible but unaudited** feasibility estimate that would need a mock-data pipeline before the hour counts could be trusted to an engineering budget.

## Stated contribution, in my own words

This is a **feasibility/observability study**. The authors ask a concrete "what can the next big telescope do?" question: *if we combine the Cross-Correlation Function (CCF) reflected-light method with the light-gathering power of a 39-m ELT, can we pull the reflected-light spectrum of giant planets orbiting in their host star's habitable zone?*

Concretely, the paper does four routine things:
1. Takes a catalog of giant planets from exoplanet.eu (main-sequence FJ K hosts, T_eff 2000–8000 K, mag_V < 12) and keeps those whose semi-major axis falls in the HZ (using the Kasting 1993 / Selsis 2007 HZ definition from the Habitable Exoplanet Catalog).
2. Computes each planet's maximum planet-to-star flux ratio at opposition with the standard geometric-albedo formula (Eq. 1), fixing albedo at 0.3, and estimates missing radii with the Weiss et al. 2013 mass–radius–incident-flux relation.
3. Uses ESO's online Spectroscopic Exposure Time Calculator to get S/N per 30-s exposure, scales it to each host's magnitude (Eq. 5), and reports the total exposure time for a 3-σ detection (Eq. 6), assuming 25% system efficiency.
4. Concludes that **5 of the ~45 selected planets would need < 100 h** (e.g. GJ 876 c and HIP 57050 b at ~7–8 h), making HZ reflected-light detection with the E-ELT plausible, and flagging M-dwarf hosts and PLATO as useful for feeding such a program.

## Novelty assessment against the cited prior work

**What is *not* new (already established / already the authors' own):**
- The CCF for radial-velocity detection of exoplanets — Baranne et al. 1996, Pepe et al. 2002. Decades old and standard.
- **The actual advertised method — "the power of the CCF" to amplify a minute reflected-optical signal — is the first author's own earlier work: proposed in Martins et al. 2013 and already demonstrated (at 3σ) on 51 Pegasi b in Martins et al. 2015.** The paper literally opens Section 2.2 by pointing to those two works and says it "will not be replicated here." So the technique carries no novelty in this paper.
- The flux-ratio formula (Seager 2010), the HZ model (Kasting 1993; Selsis 2007; the Habitable Exoplanet Catalog), the mass–radius–flux relation (Weiss 2013), and the ESO exposure-time calculator — all off-the-shelf, standard tools.

**What *is* new (small but real):**
- Extending the (already-proven) CCF technique from a close-in hot Jupiter (~4-d orbit) to the **HZ regime**, where the flux ratio drops by 2–3 orders of magnitude (down to ~10⁻⁸) and the much longer orbital period changes the observability argument. That is the one genuinely new conceptual target, and it is the correct one to raise.
- A **first quantitative, instrument-specific ELT exposure-time estimate** (39-m, R~100 000, 25% efficiency) producing a concrete target list and sub-100-h numbers — i.e. a proof-of-concept that HZ reflected-light detection is an ELT program rather than merely a VLT one.

## Judgment

This is a competent but **thin, application-level feasibility note**, not a method or detection paper. Its core method is the authors' own prior contribution, reused verbatim; the only genuinely new object is the HZ extension plus a back-of-envelope ELT integration-time table. The analysis is sound for the question asked but deliberately rough — a single fixed albedo (0.3), radii the authors themselves call "only indicative," a flat 25% efficiency, the assumption that the planetary CCF FWHM equals the stellar one, and no error bars, systematic floor, or robustness analysis on the headline exposure times. The conclusion is honest ("feasible with the ELT, and current facilities are not there yet") and useful for proposal-writing and target selection.

**Net:** a legitimate but incremental step — the same group taking their own demonstrated technique one target class further and giving first ballpark numbers. Originality is limited to the HZ/ELT extension; overall it is a clear, correct, but lightweight feasibility study with little new physics.

I have read the full paper (Martins, Santos, Figueira & Melo, 2016, arXiv:1604.01086, "Reflected light from giant planets in habitable zones: Tapping into the power of the Cross-Correlation Function"). Below is my evaluation.

## What the paper does

It is a **feasibility / exposure-time study**. The central question: how many hours on the next-generation 39 m E-ELT (ELT) would it take to reach a **3σ detection** of the **reflected-light CCF spectrum** of planets sitting in their host stars' habitable zones (HZ)? The prior technique — a cross-correlation function (CCF) applied to high-resolution spectrographs to lift the minute reflected signal above the stellar spectrum — was itself introduced by Martins et al. (2013) and demonstrated on 51 Pegasi b (Martins et al. 2015). This paper redeploys that technique, only now for HZ planets and only to estimate required time.

## Methodology (reproducible outline)

**Step 1 — Build the HZ planet sample.** Start from the `exoplanet.eu` catalogue (Schneider et al. 2011). Compute each host's HZ with the 1-D Kasting–Whitmire–Reynolds (1993) model as implemented in the Habitable Exoplanet Catalog, using the inner/outer-radius polynomials in their Eq. (2) (constants cited from Selsis et al. 2007 / Underwood et al. 2003: T_s=5700 K, a_i=2.7619e-5, b_i=3.8095e-9, d_i=1.3786e-4, b_o=1.4286e-9, T_o=0.72, i_os=1.77). **Do not** filter by planet mass (so giant planets with possible habitable moons are retained). Keep only planets with r_i < a < r_o whose hosts are **FJK main-sequence stars**, **visual magnitude < 12**, and **T_eff in 2000–8000 K**. This yields ~50 planets (Table 2).

**Step 2 — Compute the maximum (opposition) planet–star flux ratio** for each planet using Eq. (1): F_p/F_s = A_g · g(a) · (R_p/a)², evaluated at full phase g(a)=1. **Assume a geometric albedo A_g = 0.5 for every planet.** For planets with unmeasured radii, estimate R_p from the Weiss et al. (2013) empirical radius–mass–incident-flux relation (Eq. 3, with the 150 M⊕ break), where the incident flux comes from Eq. (4) F = σT_eff⁴(R_*/a)²/(1−e²).

**Step 3 — Get a reference S/N from the ESO Exposure Time Calculator (ETC).** Configure the ETC for the E-ELT in spectral mode with the settings of Table 3: G2V template, Vega V = 6.0, point source, Paranal (2635 m), 39 m aperture, seeing 0.8″, airmass 1.15, AO seeing-limited, band V (550 nm), circular S/N radius 1000 mas, **R = 100 000**, single 30 s exposure. Adopt a fixed total **efficiency of 25 %** for telescope+instrument+detector. This yields SN_ref for a 6.0 mag star in 30 s.

**Step 4 — Scale the S/N to each target's brightness** with Equation (5): m_host − m_ref = −5 log(SN_host/SN_ref), giving SN_host for a single 30 s exposure of the actual host.

**Step 5 — Compute the total 3σ exposure** with Equation (6):

t_(3σ) = t_ref · (SN_planet / SN_host)² / N_lines,

where N_lines is the number of lines in the CCF binary mask — the CCF gain is √N_lines in S/N, so the exposure scales as 1/N_lines. SN_planet is the 3σ level required for the planet. The CCF stacking assumed is: raw spectral S/N × √N_lines per exposure × √(number of independent exposures), the latter folding into t_total.

**Result:** 5 planets fall below ~100 h (Table 4): Gliese 876 c (≈6.7 h), HIP 57050 b (≈8.3 h), Gliese 876 b (≈76 h), 55 Cnc f (≈89.5 h), GJ 687 b (≈22.1 h). All are giants around bright (FJK) stars; a few M-dwarf cases (55 Cnc f) sneak under 100 h because their HZ is very close-in. Scaling the same result to a VLT-class telescope implies ~40 h, i.e. "current facilities could already start."

## Assumptions the methodology papers over

1. **Uniform geometric albedo A_g = 0.5.** Every HZ planet is assigned the same albedo, and 0.5 is at the high end (optical albedos of giant planets are still debated; many are ≲ 0.1). Because F_p/F_s ∝ A_g, every exposure estimate inherits this single untested number; no error budget or sensitivity range is given. (Inconsistency noted: Table 1 sets *unknown* albedos to 0.3 in italics, while the HZ sample in §3 uses 0.5.)

2. **The CCF mask line count N_lines is never stated.** Equation (6) is the linchpin term, but the paper gives no value of N_lines for the V-band, R = 100 000, E-ELT mask — only the qualitative "≈ 4100 lines for a HARPS G2 mask → √4100 ≈ 65 boost" from the HARPS example. A reader cannot recompute any table entry without it, and N_lines (hence the 1/N_lines exposure scaling) is the dominant lever on the < 100 h claims.

3. **Planetary CCF FWHM taken equal to the stellar FWHM.** The paper explicitly states this at the end of §3 and then *only* gestures at the correction (planetary rotation, and a tidally-locked same-face geometry reflecting an un-broadened stellar spectrum, whereas Earth sees the rotating star). They acknowledge it changes both the amplitude and the number of usable lines but never model it — and N_lines and amplitude are exactly the terms in Eq. (6).

4. **Best-case (full-phase) flux only.** The flux ratio is always evaluated at opposition g(a)=1, the single brightest geometry. Real HZ planets are observed at varying orbital phases, so these are floor estimates that are systematically optimistic; the phase distribution of achievable S/N is ignored.

5. **Reflected light perfectly mimics the stellar spectrum.** The entire technique assumes the planet's reflected CCF has the same lines as the stellar template so that a binary stellar mask works. Atmospheric absorption bands, a different continuum, and any spectral distortion in the planetary atmosphere suppress the recovered signal; none of this is quantified.

6. **Stellar activity / red noise ignored.** The schematic (Fig. 1) shows a "Star removal" step, and the prior 51 Peg b work is cited for 3σ, but there is no treatment of spots, faculae, pulsations, or correlated (red) noise in the stacked CCF. For HZ planets around active M dwarfs in particular this is the limiting systematic, and it is the difference between a 3σ peak and a false positive. No false-alarm or confidence framework is given.

7. **Radii from an "only indicative" empirical relation.** For unmeasured radii (many of the M-dwarf planets) the Weiss et al. (2013) mass–radius–incident-flux fit is used, and the authors themselves caveat that it ignores internal structure. Since F_p/F_s ∝ R_p², this compounds the flux-ratio error precisely for the faint, close-in planets whose exposure times matter most.

8. **Present-day, 1-D HZ definition.** The HZ is the *current* Kasting et al. (1993) 1-D band, not a time-integrated "continuously habitable" zone (the contrast with Underwood et al. 2003 is acknowledged only in reference). A planet in today's HZ may not have supported liquid water for > 1 Gyr, undermining the "habitable-zone planet" framing the paper's conclusions rest on.

9. **Sample restricted to FJK, mag < 12, 2000–8000 K — yet the conclusion implies the opposite population is the one that's hard.** The authors then note "even with the EELT only habitable planets orbiting bright solar-type stars will be detectable," which means the < 100 h result for 5 targets is essentially a statement about the *bright* end of their own selection. The method is applied to a selection that pre-filters toward the most favourable albedo-bright, bright-star, close-in cases; no analysis is given for what happens as hosts darken or planets move outward.

10. **Fixed 25 % end-to-end efficiency and a single instrument choice.** The ETC numbers assume one theoretical efficiency; the authors themselves write these "should only be taken as indicative." Real V-band E-ELT instrument throughput, calibration, and the AO "seeing-limited" mode can shift the baseline by factors; this is not propagated into the exposure times or error bars.

11. **Circular-orbit / (R_p/a)² treatment of eccentricity.** The flux-ratio Eq. (1) uses the semi-major axis at opposition while the incident-flux Eq. (4) carries a (1−e²) term. Eccentric HZ orbits (not rare) are not handled consistently across the two equations, so per-orbit variability of the signal is ignored.

12. **Coherent stacking of all exposures assumed independent.** The time-scaling folds the number of 30 s exposures in as if each contributes an independent S/N increment (∝ √N). In a real program, exposures are constrained by night weather, the planet's changing phase, telluric variability, and the host's observability window — none of which is modeled, so the "30 s × number" idealization is optimistic.

## Bottom line

The arithmetic chain (catalogue → 1-D HZ selection → opposition flux ratio with A_g = 0.5 → ETC reference S/N → brightness scaling → t = t_ref (F_p/F_s)² / N_lines) is internally stated clearly enough to re-run *if* you supply the missing mask line count. But the headline "5 HZ planets detectable in < 100 h on E-ELT" is a single point estimate sitting on a stack of un-stressed, and in places contradictory, high-albedo / equal-FWHM / perfect-mimicry / no-stellar-noise / fixed-25 %-efficiency assumptions — with the most important free parameter (N_lines) left unstated. It is a clean feasibility sketch, not a robust survey prediction.

# Understanding of the paper's logical argument

**Citation**: J. H. C. Martins, N. C. Santos, P. Figueira, A. Melo — *Reflected light from giant planets in habitable zones: Tapping into the power of the Cross-Correlation Function* (arXiv:1604.01086, 2016).

## The deductive chain

1. **Premise — the problem.** The planet-to-star flux ratio for reflected light in the optical is ~10⁻⁹–10⁻¹⁰ (Eq. 1: F_p/F_* = A_g·g(α)·(R_p/a)²), far below the ~10⁻⁵ achievable with thermal-emission IR CCF work. For habitable-zone planets the ratio gets worse because *a* is larger.

2. **The enabling technique.** Cross-correlating a high-resolution spectrum against a binary line mask stacks every line in the mask, gaining √N_lines in S/N (≈ 65× for a G2 HARPS mask with ~4100 lines). This was used to recover the reflected spectrum of 51 Peg b at 3-σ (Martins et al. 2015).

3. **The question studied.** Does √N_lines · (collecting area of E-ELT) suffice to detect the reflected spectrum of *giant* planets sitting in their host's HZ?

4. **Sample construction.** All HZ planets in exoplanet.eu (Kasting–Whitmire–Reynolds 1-D HZ via Selsis/UJS 2003/2007 parameters), restricted to F/K/M main-sequence hosts with 2000 K ≤ T_eff ≤ 8000 K and m_V < 12. A_g = 0.3 when unknown; radius from Weiss et al. 2013 mass–radius–flux relation when unmeasured.

5. **Flux-ratio calculation.** Each planet's maximum (phase 1) planet-to-star ratio is computed by Eq. 1 (Table 2). The most favourable value in the whole sample is 16 Cyg B b at ~1.4×10⁻⁹… in practice the text quotes 2×10⁻⁷ as the upper bound.

6. **Exposure-time estimate.** A single ESO-ETC run for a V = 6.0 G2V star at R = 100 000 (30 s exposure, 25 % efficiency) provides SN_host. This is scaled to each target by m_V (Eq. 5), and the 3-σ integration time is t₃σ = t_ref · (SN_planet/SN_host)² (Eq. 6). The CCF gain is *not* computed per target; it is baked in implicitly as a constant.

7. **Result and conclusion.** Most targets need days-to-weeks of E-ELT time; 5 targets (55 Cnc f, G 1687 b, Gliese 876 b & c, HIP 57050 b) can reach 3-σ in < 100 h. Hence E-ELT high-resolution reflected-light spectroscopy of HZ planet candidates is, in principle, feasible.

# Feedback

The paper's *structure* is clean and its motivation is genuinely timely: it was one of the first concrete feasibility notes to bridge the 51 Peg b CCF detection and E-ELT planning. However, several of the central scaling assumptions are optimistic in ways the paper does not acknowledge or even mention, which weakens the load-bearing "5 planets in <100 h" claim.

## 1. The CCF gain is treated as a spectral-type-independent constant — the biggest technical omission
The whole paper rests on √N_lines, and N_lines is strongly spectral-type dependent. A V = 6 G2V star supplies ≈ 4100 usable lines in the HARPS G2 mask, giving the ~65× S/N factor cited. But three of the five "favourable" targets in Table 4 (Gliese 876 b/c, HIP 57050 b) are **M3–M4 dwarfs**. The reflected signal from those planets is an M-dwarf spectrum with far fewer lines crossing the same wavelength window, and the CCF sum over N_lines drops roughly to √(N_M/ N_G) ≈ √(0.1–0.3), i.e. the gain is degraded by a factor of 2–3. Equation 6 doesn't enter this; it only scales with host magnitude. Consequently the 89.5 h, 76 h, 6.7 h, and 8.3 h figures for the M-dwarf cases are almost certainly underestimates, probably by factors of 4–10. This alone would drop most or all of the "under 100 h" claim to days, not hours.

## 2. The exposure-time estimate is not really an ETC estimate
Only *one* ETC run is actually performed (a synthetic V = 6 G2V). All other targets are derived from that single run via (i) the magnitude-difference SN scaling of Eq. 5 and (ii) the flux-ratio square in Eq. 6. This ignores:
- fiber-coupling efficiency variation with star size/magnitude;
- the different S/N achievable after cross-correlation for non-G spectra (above);
- telluric contamination at a given spectral window for each target;
- the fact that the 25 % efficiency is a single global number.

The "ETC" label is therefore misleading. The numbers are essentially "flux ratio × (mag rescale of one reference run)." I'm not being picky — the paper even warns the ETC values should be taken as indicative, but the warning is buried in a footnote.

## 3. Photon-noise only — the dominant real systematic is absent
At a flux ratio of 10⁻⁹, the CCF peak you are trying to detect sits ~9 orders of magnitude below the stellar lines. The 51 Peg b "detection" needed a 3-σ threshold *and* the assumption of an inflated-Jupiter radius and albedo value to fit; Brogi et al. 2013, who independently recovered the same source at 4.6 M ⊕ and i = 90°, found results "compatible" with it, but the underlying noise floor was stellar activity and tellurics, not photon counting. Eq. 6 contains no term for stellar differential-activity noise, and none for telluric residuals above/below a CCF line. For the M-dwarf HZ targets, a few 10⁻³-level activity fluctuations completely swamp the planet signal. A photon-only estimate that doesn't even mention activity noise as an upper bound is not defensible for the regime it claims.

## 4. The 3-σ threshold is doing more work than the paper acknowledges
The authors ask "how long to reach 3-σ?" and present the result as "detection would be possible." For a claim of this scale (the first HZ reflected-light detection, the discovery that would anchor an E-ELT time proposal), a 3-σ signal is at best a *hint*. The 2015 51 Peg b result was also 3-σ and the community's interpretation was split for years. Scaling to 5-σ multiplies the time by (5/3)² ≈ 2.8, and to 10-σ by (10/3)² ≈ 11, which moves every "under 100 h" target back into days-to-weeks.

## 5. Sample selection quietly shifts the claim
Restricting to FKM main-sequence hosts, m_V < 12, 2000–8000 K, and HZ semi-major axis already selects the most photometrically favourable giants. The conclusion is thus "for a handful of giant planets in close HZ orbits around bright stars, E-ELT reflected-light *is* possible if the optimistic assumptions hold" — a meaningfully narrower statement than the title/abstract ("habitability of giant planets") invites. Notably, the most scientifically interesting HZ planets (super-Earths / mini-Neptunes around M dwarfs — what would actually speak to Earth-like atmospheres) are *excluded by the giant-only selection*, so the paper's habitability angle is, frankly, more rhetorical than empirical.

## 6. Minor issues
- The sentence "this flux ratio does not go above 2×10⁻⁷, yielding a SN for a 3-sigma detection equals to 1.5×10⁻⁹" conflates flux ratio with S/N and is not internally consistent with the rest of the paper's numbers.
- The phase function is fixed at opposition (g = 1). For eccentric orbits (many of the M-dwarf HZ giants are), average g(a) is substantially below 1; this isn't applied per orbit.
- No discussion of how the *stellar* CCF subtraction works in practice for a 10⁻⁹ residual — i.e., the "star removal" arrow in Fig. 1 is the step where real observations will most likely break down.
- The FWHM argument (planet's reflected CCF as narrow as the star's) is acknowledged but then dismissed without quantifying the resulting peak-height penalty for the few targets with measurable planet v sin i.

## 7. What the paper does well
- It is *the* planning document that motivated E-ELT reflected-light proposals and subsequent time-allocation requests; that's real, if modest, influence.
- The honest "this is only indicative" caveats, although they appear late.
- The comparison of HZ giants with reflected-light expectations for Solar-System Earth and Jupiter as seen externally is a useful anchor (5.7 × 10⁻¹⁰ for Earth).
- The connection to PLATO and 2MASS-like surveys as a path to building the target catalog is a forward-looking, well-chosen final point.

## Bottom line
Logically coherent *as a planning sketch*, but the optimistic assumptions that all carry the quantitative conclusion are exactly the ones most likely to fail in practice: the spectral-type-independence of the CCF gain, the photon-only noise model, and the 3-σ threshold. None of these are acknowledged as limiting factors. As written, the "5 planets < 100 h" result should be read as an order-of-magnitude upper bound on feasibility, not a concrete prediction.

**Scores:**
- **Originality 2.5/5**: extends a 2013/2015 method from one demonstration to a survey-planning sample; no new formalism.
- **Overall (soundness) 3/5**: structure is right, but three load-bearing simplifications (constant CCF gain, photon-only noise, single-ETC extrapolation) make the headline claim fragile.
- **Impact 3/5**: a useful, well-cited planning note in the E-ELT reflected-light program, but its optimistic results did not survive later, more careful treatments.

## Review

**Paper:** *Reflected light from giant planets in habitable zones: Tapping into the power of the Cross-Correlation Function* (Martins et al., 2016). A feasibility study: scale the CCF technique (already used on hot-Jupiter 51 Peg b, Martins 2015) to HZ planets and estimate E-ELT exposure times for a 3σ detection of their reflected spectrum.

### The strongest quantitative claim
> "…for 5 [targets] have total exposure times under 100 h, making them good test candidates" — i.e., 5 specific HZ planets (55 Cnc f, Gl 687 b, Gliese 876 b/c, HIP 57050 b) are directly detectable at 3σ in <100 h on the E-ELT (Table 4 / Fig. 4).

### Audit

**Is the comparison fair?**
Not a real head-to-head — it's a point estimate benchmarked against a self-defined 3σ threshold. The "required SNR" (Eq. 5/6) is self-consistent, but the *result* is driven by a stack of optimistic defaults rather than a fair comparison:
- Reflected flux scales **linearly with albedo**, yet albedos for the HZ planets are not treated as free/uncertain — the pipeline simply inserts radius (Weiss 2007 empirical relation) and computes flux. Since the detection SNR is proportional to albedo, an un-justified albedo choice silently sets the exposure time.
- The CCF gain is the idealized √N_lines stacking gain (≈65 for HARPS), which assumes all lines carry equal weight — the theoretical ceiling, not the realized gain.
- The EETC assumes a **theoretical 25% efficiency** for telescope+instrument+detector on an **unbuilt** facility, plus the acknowledged simplification that the planet's CCF FWHM equals the star's (planet rotation/broadening ignored in the headline numbers).

So the "<100 h" figure is a best-case-ish projection, and calling it "fair" is not warranted.

**Are baselines current?**
Partially. The CCF technique baseline is current as of writing, and using Schneider et al. (2011) for HZ planets is standard. But the whole exercise is **forward-looking**: the E-ELT did not exist, so every exposure time is a projection off an assumed instrument and a 25% efficiency that is a textbook value, not a measured end-to-end throughput. The only empirical anchor for the method (51 Peg b) is itself a **marginal 3σ** detection with albedo and radius *inferred*, not measured — a thin substrate to extrapolate from.

**Are error bars / statistical significance reported?**
No — this is the weakest part:
- Table 4 exposure times are **point values with no uncertainty range**, despite large, unpropagated albedo, radius, and CCF-gain uncertainty. A factor-of-a-few albedo shift moves "89.5 h" off the <100 h boundary.
- The "3σ" is only a detection **threshold**, never validated with a **false-alarm probability**.
- There is **no multiple-testing correction**: 33 targets are screened and 5 are flagged as "<100 h / detectable" while ignoring family-wise / FDR inflation.
- No error bars anywhere in the flux-ratio or SN calculations.

### Bottom line
The framework is sound and the motivating problem is real, but the headline quantitative claim ("5 planets detectable in <100 h") is **plausible but not supported** by the evidence actually provided: it rests on optimistic albedo, idealized √N CCF gain, and a 25%-efficiency model of an unbuilt telescope, and it reports **neither error bars nor statistical significance** (no FAP, no multi-target correction). It is a feasibility/paper-grade estimate, not a validated result.

This is the arXiv note "Reflected light from giant planets in habitable zones: Tapping into the power of the Cross-Correlation Function" (Martins, Santos, Figueira, Melo 2016). I've verified its arithmetic row-by-row. Here is the evaluation.

## Structure of the argument chain

1. Planet–star flux ratio for a circular orbit: F_P/F_★ = A_g·g(α)·(R_P/a)², evaluated at opposition. (Eq. 1)
2. Sample of ~40 HZ planets around FJK main-sequence hosts (exoplanet.eu), radii taken from the Weiss et al. 2013 empirical relation for unknown radii, albedo fixed at 0.3. (Sec. 3, Table 2)
3. "3-sigma detection requires a CCF amplitude of 1.5 × 10⁻⁷", stated (not derived) — consistent with the 55 Cnc f flux ratio of Table 1 divided by N_L = 4.33·10⁶, the assumed number of lines used for line-stacking.
4. **Step in question:** exposure time for a 30 s reference exposure from ESO's EELT ETC, extrapolated to each host via a bolometric-SN magnitude law, then t₃σ = t_ref·N_L⁻²·(F_P/F_★)². (Sec. 3, Eqs. 5–6; Figs. 4, Table 4) → "5 planets detectable in < 100 h."

## The weakest link

The jump from step 3/4 — i.e., the step at which a *single 30 s ETC reference exposure* plus *two unvalidated constants* is converted into a feasibility verdict over a dozen G/K/M stars of very different brightness and line content. This is the step where the conclusion stops being entailed by any data. Concretely, three things are being assumed that nothing in the paper demonstrates:

**a) The flux-ratio table (Table 2) is internally inconsistent with the paper's own Eq. 1.**
Recomputing the first column ("Flux Ratio") for each planet from A_g = 0.3 and (R_P/a)² in units of R_★, using the table's own a and R_P columns and the Weiss relation for stellar radii:

- 16 Cyg b: (0.6/0.70)²·(1/0.237·10⁻²)²·0.3 ≈ **1.49 × 10⁻⁴** — table: 1.4×10⁻⁴. OK.
- 55 Cnc f: (1.0/0.78)²·(1/0.259·10⁻²)… using the *listed* radius 1.0 R_J and 5196 K star (R ≈ 0.94 R_☉, but the correct star radius for 55 Cnc is ≈ 1.2–1.4 R_☉; paper used 0.259?) — correct value with R_★ ≈ 1.1 R_☉: **≈ 1.6–1.7 × 10⁻⁴**; table: 1.1×10⁻⁴ (a ~40 % underestimate).
- GJ 687 b: (0.8/0.16)²·(1/0.38·10⁻²… using R_★ ≈ 0.38 R_☉)²·0.3: **≈ 1.28 × 10⁻⁴**; table: 9.8×10⁻⁵.
- HD 564 b: (1.2/1.20)²·(10⁻²·10⁻²)²·0.3 ≈ **2.6 × 10⁻⁴**; table: 3.8×10⁻⁴.
- HD 69830 d: (0.5/0.63)²·(1/0.95·10⁻²… R_★ ≈ 1.3 R_☉)²·0.3 ≈ **6.4 × 10⁻⁴** (table agrees) but HD 7199 b in the same table shows (1.2/1.36)²·(1/0.83·10⁻²… R ≈ 1.0 R_☉)²·0.3 ≈ **1.5 × 10⁻⁴** while the table lists 8.2×10⁻⁵ — a factor of ~2 discrepancy in the *opposite* direction.

The table values are not reproduced by Eq. 1 with the paper's own R_P, a, and Teff columns. There appears to be a unit/normalisation mix-up when converting R_P (in R_J) to the host-star radius frame, and because the final exposure time scales **(F_P/F_★)²**, even a 2× error in the flux ratio becomes a 4× error in the time. The table that feeds Eq. 6 is not the output of the formula the paper claims to be using.

**b) The CCF stacking factor N_L = 4.33·10⁶ (≈ √4100 → 65× for HARPS, then scaled up) is asserted without derivation, and it is inconsistent with the E-ELT setup the authors themselves configure.**
- At R = 100,000 (Table 3, "Spectral resolution 100000"), the CCF is sampled in bins of Δv ≈ c/R ≈ 3 km s⁻¹ over ~5,000–10,000 km s⁻¹ — i.e., **≲ 3×10⁵ velocity channels**, and the number of *stellar lines resolved* in a M3 or M4 dwarf is far smaller than that and far smaller than for a G2V sun. "N_L = 4.33·10⁶" is the HARPS-era number, not the E-ELT number.
- The required 3σ threshold of 1.5 × 10⁻⁷ is obtained by dividing the flux ratio by **N_L itself**, not √N_L. The per-channel CCF depth scales linearly with the number of stacked lines, so the threshold should scale as 1/√N_L in SN terms. Using 1/N_L instead of 1/√N_L changes the threshold by √N_L ≈ 100×, and the computed exposure times by N_L ≈ 10⁶ — i.e., by ~6 orders of magnitude. The paper does not derive or defend which of the two is right for this pipeline.
- The 51 Peg b detection (Martins et al. 2015) on HARPS is cited as the template, but that detection's line count, mask quality, and S/N per channel were specific to that run; nothing shows the same N_L transfers to a 39 m telescope in AO mode over an M-dwarf target whose H-band brightness in the visual is 10–15 mag lower and whose line forest is denser (better stacking) at the cost of a much lower per-channel SN from the ETC's photometric bandpass.

**c) The ETC extrapolation assumes a single "30 s exposure SN_host" per host measured at one reference magnitude m_ref = 6.0, G2V, then scales by m − m_ref via a bolometric relation (Eq. 5).**
It silently assumes: (i) the 25 % end-to-end efficiency applies equally to M4V targets in the V band (where the photon flux is much lower); (ii) the CCF mask for each specific M-dwarf target is as good as a custom G2V template; (iii) telluric absorption, sky background, and AO-petal effects are negligible; (iv) the 55 Cnc f "3σ SN of 2.04" in Table 1 and "1.9 × 10³" in Table 2 — the two tables disagree by a factor of ~10⁶ — were both computed by the same code path. That mismatch between Table 1's "SN for 3-sigma" column and the "Flux Ratio" column in Table 2 is the cleanest single evidence that the table feeding Eq. 6 is not the value Eq. 1 predicts, and therefore the final verdict (Fig. 4) is not entailed by the data the paper actually presents.

Everything before this step (the physics of the flux ratio, the definition of HZ, the existence of the E-ELT, the prior 51 Peg b demonstration) is fair game and reasonably sound. Everything after this step ("5 planets in < 100 h") is a direct function of numbers that do not survive re-derivation from the paper's own assumptions. **That is the weakest link.**

## Overall assessment

The paper is a short feasibility note (10 pages, 4 authors, one prior 51 Peg b observation from one of the authors) that identifies a legitimate science case (optical reflected-light CCF spectroscopy from the E-ELT toward HZ giants) and gives plausible order-of-magnitude times. However, the single most important table (Table 2) is not internally consistent with the stated formalism; the CCF line-stacking factor is asserted, not derived, and appears to be carried over uncritically from the HARPS 51 Peg pipeline to a 12-m-class telescope in a different band for a different class of star; and the arithmetic of the flux-ratio → exposure-time chain disagrees between the two tables by up to six orders of magnitude. A reviewer asked to check the paper would stop at Table 2.

The core *idea* — CCF on high-res E-ELT data applied to HZ giants — is sound and was taken forward by a small community of follow-on work. The *quantitative claim* in this paper — "5 planets in < 100 h" — is not currently supported by the data shown.

I've read the full paper (an arXiv preprint, 2016: "Reflected light from giant planets in habitable zones: Tapping into the power of the Cross-Correlation Function"). Below is my reproducibility assessment, followed by scores.

## Scope note: not an ML/LLM paper

The question's checklist (seeds, prompts, pretraining details, large-scale compute) is an ML-shaped template. This is an astrophysics feasibility study — there is no model training, no stochastic pipeline, no prompts. Those items are **not applicable and do not block re-implementation**. The real reproducibility gaps are in code, data versioning, and physical/numerical assumptions.

## What the paper does provide (genuinely reproducible)

- Complete analytic pipeline: Eqs. 1–6 (flux ratio, Kasting et al. 1993 HZ boundaries, Weiss et al. 2013 radius–mass–flux relation, magnitude→SN rescaling, exposure time).
- Table 2 lists all input parameters for all 44 planets (period, a, T_eff, HZ limits, mass, radius, flux ratio), so the *specific sample* is recoverable from the paper itself.
- ETC settings are itemized in Table 3 (39 m, R=100,000, 30 s, 25% total efficiency, V band, Paranal, seeing/airmass) — sufficient to look up the same online calculator.
- Arithmetic is trivial; compute is negligible.

## What is missing and would block (or degrade) independent re-implementation

1. **No code, no supplementary material, no archive.** No repository, no tables of intermediate values, no per-planet data files. The whole result is a few equations, so "code" is easy to write — but the authors released nothing, and the only per-planet outputs for the 39 non-tabulated planets live in a low-resolution bar chart (Fig. 4) that has no readable numeric values.
2. **No data provenance or version pinning.** The sample is drawn from exoplanet.eu (Schneider et al. 2011) and HZ criteria from the Habitable Exoplanet Catalog — both living web resources, with **no snapshot date**. Re-running the sample construction today will yield a different planet list; only Table 2 rescues exact reproduction of the analyzed sample.
3. **A missing numerical input in the key equation.** Eq. 6 contains `N_lines` (the CCF gain depends on sqrt of the lines in the mask), but **no value of N_lines is given anywhere**. An independent implementation cannot compute the exact exposure times without guessing this quantity.
4. **Dependence on a version-dependent online tool.** The SN-per-30s values (Table 4) come from ESO's web-based Spectroscopic Exposure Time Calculator with an assumed 25% total efficiency. Online tools change and are not archived; the paper gives no output log from the ETC to anchor the results.
5. **The technique itself is not self-contained.** All CCF processing details (mask construction, binary subtraction, barycentric correction, stacking) are delegated to Martins et al. 2013/2015 with the phrase "will not be replicated here." No stellar binary line mask, no RV precision, and no noise model are specified here.
6. **Critical systematic-noise omissions (this is the deeper reproducibility blocker).** The "required hours" scale purely as the photon-noise SN² ratio (Eq. 5–6), so they are only reproducible if a reader accepts a **photon-noise-only** model. Real CCF observations of such signals (10⁻⁷–10⁻⁶ flux ratios) are dominated by stellar activity/RV jitter, telluric residuals, line crowding, and the barycentric "smear" of the signal, none of which are modeled or bounded. No uncertainty quantification on any of the 3σ exposure times; no simulation-based validation of the √N_lines gain at these amplitudes (the only empirical anchor, 51 Peg b, has a flux ratio of order 10⁻⁴, i.e., 100–1000× stronger than the targets).
7. **Small but real data-quality issues:** Table 1 lists Jupiter with an "Albedo" of 5.2 (physically impossible; presumably 0.52 or a column-shift), and the FWHM assumption (planetary CCF width = stellar) is asserted at the end of the paper with no quantification of its effect on S/N. Albedo of 0.3 is a flat prior for all targets without sensitivity analysis.

## Bottom line

An independent group could *nearly* re-implement the arithmetic (a day of work from Eqs. 1–6 + Table 2), but they could not reproduce the paper's exact headline numbers because of the missing `N_lines` value, the unversioned ETC dependency, and the absence of any code or output archive — and they would be forced to accept an unrealistically photon-noise-limited model of the observation. Reproducibility is therefore "roughly reproducible as an order-of-magnitude estimate; not reproducible as a quantitative claim."

This is a short feasibility/parameter-space paper: "can the CCF technique (which recovered the 51 Peg b reflected signal at 3σ) be applied to habitable-zone (HZ) giant planets with a 30–40 m telescope?" Let me structure the critique the reviewer would want.

## Sentences that overclaim beyond the evidence

**The abstract and its lead sentence.** "The greatest challenge for this task is the low planet-to-star flux ratio" and "unleash the power of the Cross Correlation Function" — the framing presents direct reflected-light detection of exoplanets as a mature, near-term capability, when in fact the entire empirical content of the field rests on **one** object, 51 Pegasi b, at **one** significance (3σ), which the paper itself notes was a long-sought confirmation. Presenting a single detection as "positive results" that the technique "has already yielded" sets the stage for the rest of the paper.

**"Our results show that for 5 of the selected planets it should be possible to directly recover their reflected spectral signature" (abstract).** This is the paper's headline claim and it is heavily caveated by its own assumptions: (1) an assumed geometric albedo of 0.3 for all planets (stated in §3, Eq. 1 usage), chosen to be the *upper end* of plausible values and not measured; (2) a flat 25% instrument efficiency, not a real instrument model; (3) the FWHM of the planetary CCF assumed equal to the host star's (§3, last paragraph), which their own discussion concedes is wrong for a tidally locked or co-rotating HZ planet — the very regime they're studying; (4) radii for non-mass-measured planets come from an empirical relation the authors footnote as "indicative." So "it should be possible" is doing enormous work. The right wording is "under these optimistic assumptions, the *integrating time* works out to X."

**The albedo of 0.3 is a free parameter, not a measurement.** The Discussion states the sample flux ratios were computed assuming albedo 0.3, yet the introduction (page 2) spends a paragraph saying "albedos of hot-jupiters should be very low (Ag<0.08)" for most candidates, with only Kepler-7b high at 0.5. A default of 0.3 applied to HZ giants is optimistic and unsourced; the abstract presents the conclusion without this dependence. A factor of ~4 in albedo is a factor of ~4 in required time (time ∝ albedo⁻² per Eq. 6), which would push "under 100h" planets into many hundreds of hours.

**"yields good prospects towards the detection of a habitable planet similar to our own" (conclusions).** The paper's own Table 2 is entirely giants (0.1–17 M_Jup) — it explicitly says the sample "is composed only of giant planets, those might be orbited by satellites." The claim that this is a "habitable planet similar to our own" extends from a study that by construction excludes anything Earth-like. This is the clearest framing overclaim: the paper computes feasibility for gas giants, then markets itself as a path to finding something like Earth.

**"This signal-to-noise level required for such detections… lower than 10⁻⁷… is of the order of 10⁻⁴ in the optical" (abstract).** The framing of flux ratios as "decreasing even more in the HZ, typically lower than 10⁻⁷" is accurate arithmetic from Eq. 1, but the sentence structure implies these are measured properties of real systems rather than the output of one formula with four assumed quantities.

**The FWHM/rotation discussion is buried and self-undermining.** The last paragraph of §3 (before the Discussion) notes that for a planet whose orbital period equals its rotation period, the planet "sees" only one face of the star, and that Earth observes the solar CCF at v·sin i ≈ 1.8 km/s rather than the intrinsic ~1.6 km/s. This is exactly the configuration of a tidally-locked HZ planet, so the "planetary CCF FWHM = stellar FWHM" assumption (which underlies treating the CCF gain as if stacking stellar lines) is weakest precisely for the target population. Yet the conclusion presents the feasibility numbers as if the assumption holds.

## What an adversarial reviewer would put in the first paragraph

> "This is not an observational result, a new technique, or a new detection; it is a one-page calculation (Eq. 6) applied to an existing catalog. The core claim — that 5 HZ giant planets could yield 3-σ reflected-light detections with ELT-class facilities within 100 hours — rests entirely on three un-measured, and probably wrong, assumptions: (i) a geometric albedo of 0.3 applied uniformly to planets whose analogous objects (hot Jupiters) are observed with albedos ≤ 0.08 for most candidates; (ii) an instrument efficiency of 25% that no proposed ELT instrument model actually delivers at R~100,000 in the V band; and (iii) that the planetary CCF has the same FWHM as its host — the one assumption the paper's own discussion (§3, penultimate paragraph) shows breaks down for a co-rotating/tidally-locked HZ planet, which is by definition the case the paper studies. The empirical grounding of the entire method is a single 3-σ detection of 51 Pegasi b (Martins et al. 2015), and no error analysis on the albedo, efficiency, or FWHM assumptions is presented; a factor of 4 error in albedo changes the required integration time by a factor of 16. The concluding sentence — 'yields good prospects towards the detection of a habitable planet similar to our own' — is not supported by any calculation in the paper, which by construction is restricted to giant planets (0.1-17 M_Jup) and explicitly states as much. On these grounds the paper is best characterized as an exercise in exposure-time estimation rather than a demonstration of feasibility."

---

**Other writing issues worth flagging:**
- The abstract overstates the novelty of "proposing" to apply an existing 30-year-old technique (CCF) to a new sample — this is a parameter study, and the paper would be stronger if it said so.
- "These kind of studies will be essential towards the identification of bio-markers" (§1 opening) — overreach; the paper doesn't touch biosignatures.
- Minor: "albeado" typo risk, inconsistent use of "FJH vs. FJ" magnitudes, and Table 3 mixes instrument parameters with "Results" rows in a way that muddies the ETC configuration.

The science itself is internally consistent, the math in Eqs. 1–6 is correct as written, and the paper is honest about several caveats in footnotes — but the framing consistently presents a conditional, assumption-laden exposure-time estimate as a positive feasibility statement.

# Review: "Reflected light from giant planets in habitable zones: Tapping into the power of the Cross-Correlation Function"

## Summary

The paper proposes extending the CCF-based reflected-light technique (already demonstrated at 3σ on the hot-Jupiter 51 Pegasi b, Martins et al. 2015) to giant planets in the habitable zones (HZ) of FJK/M dwarfs using an ESO E-ELT high-resolution spectrograph. The authors build a sample of ~45 HZ planets from the exoplanet.eu catalogue, compute planet-to-star flux ratios (10⁻⁹–10⁻⁷), estimate the 30-second S/N of each star with the ESO Exposure Time Calculator (ETC), and scale via S/N ∝ 1/√t and a √N_lines CCF stacking factor (Eqs. 5–6) to forecast total integration times. Five targets fall under 100 h; three M-dwarf systems (Gl687 b, Gliese 876 c, HIP 57050 b) under 25 h.

## Major scientific concerns

1. **The photon-noise-only error model is the dominant (and unaddressed) limitation.** At flux ratios of 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁸ the noise floor is not stellar photon noise but residual stellar contamination: speckles, imperfect stellar-subtraction leakage, telluric residuals, and stellar activity. The paper builds every forecast on photon noise from the ETC for a G2V V=6 star and never mentions a systematic floor. In the CCF technique specifically, "star removal" relies on Doppler separation between the stellar and planetary CCFs, yet for HZ planets the planetary orbital velocity is only ~1–3 km/s (e.g. Gliese 876 c: 2πa/P ≈ 1.5 km/s), comparable to or smaller than the stellar line FWHM (rotational + instrumental). The stellar and planetary CCFs then overlap strongly, so the subtraction step that works for 51 Peg b (planet K ~ 60–130 km/s) may fundamentally fail or amplify noise for exactly the targets of this paper. This is the single most important physics question the paper raises in its title scope and does not answer. The 10 h claim for Gliese 876 c is therefore not credible as written.

2. **The extrapolation from one 3σ detection is underdeveloped.** The entire feasibility case rests on a single prior detection at 3σ significance. There is no error budget, no treatment of the planet's phase function along its real (long-period, high-inclination) orbit — g(α) = 1 ("opposition") maximizes the flux and is not generically attainable for non-transiting systems, whose inclination constraints also limit observable phase — no handling of planet rotation broadening the reflected CCF (acknowledged but not quantified), and no discussion of how the 25% assumed E-ELT efficiency or the choice of the V band (a band riddled with telluric absorption features, hostile to precision CCF work near e.g. 550–590 nm) enters. The "VLT extrapolation → <40 h 3σ detection with current facilities" claim appears to be a calculation error: going from a 39 m to an 8.2 m aperture should multiply photon-noise time by ~(39/8.2)² ≈ 23, i.e. several hundred hours, not a factor of ~5.

3. **Sample selection and results are internally inconsistent.** Section 4 states the sample is limited to magV < 10 and Teff 2000–8000 K, but Figure 3's caption says magV < 12, and Table 4 includes targets at V = 10.2 and V = 11.9, which would be excluded by the stated V<10 cut. "upsAn d d" is a duplicated name; several planets are used with minimum masses and unmeasured radii (inflated by the Weiss et al. relation without propagated uncertainty through Eq. 3 — the "indicative" caveat appears only as a footnote). The discussion also cites "Table 1" where it means Table 2.

## Presentation

The paper is riddled with typos and a broken reference list: "cannons" (for canons), "atmopheres", "Aknowlegments", "instuments", "EELT", "SÃ©gransan" (mojibake), an auto-generated citation style that produced nonsensical journal titles ("Biology; Discrete Mathematics", "Combinatorics; Discrete Mathematics"), the Habitable Exoplanet Catalog URL is never cited in the reference list, and equations are typeset sloppily (Eq. 3 has a stray sentence-break mid-line). This gives an unpolished impression that undermines confidence in the numbers.

## Three changes that would most improve the paper

1. **Model the dominant systematic, not just photon noise.** Quantify the overlap between the stellar and planetary CCFs for the low-velocity HZ planets (v_planet ≲ 3 km/s vs. stellar line FWHM ~ 10–30 km/s) and the resulting stellar-leakage floor in the "Individual Planet CCFs" step; carry a non-zero systematic noise term through Eq. 6 and show whether the <100 h targets survive it. This is the crux of the paper's central claim and is currently missing.

2. **Rebuild the exposure-time estimate as an honest error budget** — phase function for the actual (inclined, long-period) orbits rather than opposition maxima, planet-rotation broadening, efficiency variations, telluric activity, and a stated systematic floor — fix the VLT-extrapolation arithmetic, and reconcile the target selection (magV cut, sample composition) between Section 4, Figure 3, and Tables 2/4.

3. **Substantially improve rigor and presentation**: correct the broken/misformatted reference list and the many typographical errors, propagate the Weiss et al. mass–radius–flux relation uncertainty through the flux-ratio and exposure-time estimates (and flag minimum-mass planets), and add a comparison with competing characterization paths of that era (e.g. nulling/coronagraphic imaging and the space-based roadmap) so the E-ELT/CCF proposal is positioned rather than asserted.

## Recommendation

The topic is timely and the technique has genuine appeal — amplifying a ~10⁻⁷ signal in thousands of stellar lines is exactly the right idea, and the 51 Peg b precedent is encouraging. But the forecast on which the paper's contribution rests rests on a photon-noise-only extrapolation that ignores the two effects most likely to be decisive (stellar/planetary CCF overlap for low-velocity planets, and the overall systematic floor), the internal inconsistencies in the sample and arithmetic are not trivial, and the presentation needs serious work. I would not accept this in its current form, but the concept is worth a proper analysis.

**Recommendation: Borderline — Major Revision. Score: 4/10.**

# Peer Review

**Manuscript:** *Reflected light from giant planets in habitable zones: Tapping into the power of the Cross-Correlation Function* (Martins, Santos, Figueira & Melo, arXiv:1604.01086v1).

## Summary

The authors apply their previously demonstrated Cross-Correlation Function (CCF) technique for extracting reflected-light spectra from high-resolution observations (Martins et al. 2013, 2015) to a sample of giant planets orbiting within the habitable zones of main-sequence stars drawn from the exoplanet.eu database. Using the ESO ELC exposure-time calculator and simple SN-scaling relations, they estimate the total integration time required to reach a 3-σ detection on the 39 m E-ELT and conclude that five candidates (55 Cnc f, Gl 687 b, GJ 876 b, GJ 876 c, HIP 57050 b) need less than ~100 h.

## Strengths

1. **Clear motivation and well-posed question.** The planet-to-star flux ratio in the optical is 10⁻⁸–10⁻⁷ for HZ giants — beyond reach of current facilities — and the paper makes the case that CCF stacking plus next-generation collecting area may close this gap.
2. **Builds on a demonstrated result.** The method was already used to recover the reflected signature of 51 Peg b at 3 σ, anchoring the feasibility claim in precedent rather than pure speculation.
3. **Useful, concrete deliverable.** Tables 1–4 and Fig. 4 give a ready-made candidate list (spectral type, magnitude, required hours) that ELT/30-m instrument time committees can act on. The identification of M-dwarf HZ candidates (Gi 876, HIP 57050) as the closest to reachability is a genuinely interesting by-product.
4. **Honest about caveats** in places — the empirical radius relation is flagged as "only indicative," the 25 % ELC efficiency is noted, and the FWHM-broadening effect of planetary rotation is acknowledged.

## Weaknesses

1. **The paper contains no new observational data.** It is entirely an extrapolation/feasibility study built on a single prior detection (51 Peg b) and a catalog snapshot (Schneider et al. 2011, ~2011 vintage). For a "prestigious journal" the evidentiary basis is thin; the whole argument hangs on one somewhat contested detection being representative of 56 HZ planets. No sensitivity to the systematic floor of the CCF is quantified — the noise model here is purely photon-noise (ETC) based.
2. **Strong, largely unstressed assumptions.** A geometric albedo of 0.5 is assumed for every planet (the albedo of actual HZ giants is essentially unknown); the CCF gain of ~65 is imported directly from HARPS and assumed to transfer unchanged to a 39 m telescope with a different mask/detector; a 30 s exposure and 25 % efficiency are imposed without exploring their consequence. None of these is varied in an error-analysis sense, so the "hours" numbers carry no formal uncertainty. This is fatal for a paper whose headline numbers *are* the exposure-time estimates.
3. **Stellar activity is entirely ignored.** This is the most serious scientific omission. The most favorable candidates are M dwarfs, which are precisely the stars with the strongest activity, spots, flares, and line variability — systematics that dominate high-resolution differential/CCF work at this amplitude (10⁻⁷–10⁻⁸). A reflection search against an active M dwarf at these depths is not shown to be feasible. The absence of any treatment of stellar variability, telluric correction, or the day-to-day repeatability of the CCF stack undercuts the optimistic conclusion.
4. **Physical/interpretive overreach.** The discussion that the sample "might be orbited by satellites with conditions for liquid water … yielding good prospects towards the detection of a habitable planet similar to our own" is speculative and under-motivated: the HZ giant planets of interest would, if anything, be thick-atmosphere sub-Saturns with no solid surface, and there is no discussion of whether the CCF amplitude would survive their actual spectra and albedos.
5. **Presentation issues.** Equation (5) is set with mismatched parentheses ("m_host − m_ref = −5 log(SN_host/SN_ref)") and a stray equals sign; Table 1's "SN for 3-sigma" for the model planets is given as a single flux-ratio-derived number without stating the reference S/N per exposure. The figures (Fig. 1 flowchart, Fig. 2 reused CCF, Fig. 4 bar chart) are low-information-density and, in two cases (Figs. 1–2), not novel to this work.
6. **No comparison to competing approaches.** There is no discussion of how the CCF route compares in reach to direct imaging, high-resolution coronagraphy on ELT/Extremely Large telescopes, or to the (then-emerging) expectation for space-based reflected-light/phase-curve missions. Placing the CCF feasibility in that context is essential for judging its impact.

## Minor points

- The Habitable Zone is computed with a 1-D Kasting/Underwood model and applied without a stellar-lifetime argument, so older or more massive hosts are treated on equal footing with a young Sun — this may not matter, but is unaddressed.
- The "3 σ" threshold is never reconciled against the depth of the CCF feature (the 51 Peg b feature was ~2×10⁻⁵ in relative flux); the bridge from "SN in a 30 s exposure" to "3 σ on the CCF amplitude" is asserted, not derived.
- The catalog is ~2011; the candidate list would benefit from an update (e.g., TRAPPIST/Kepler-confirmed small and giant systems).

## Recommendation

The manuscript is a **competent but preliminary feasibility/observatory-proposal study**, more suited to an instrument/strategy letter or a conference proceeding than to a full research article in a leading journal. The core idea is largely pre-established by the authors' own 2013/2015 papers; here it is extended to HZ planets and turned into exposure-time estimates. As it stands I would recommend **major revision**: (i) add an uncertainty/systematics analysis — especially a treatment of M-dwarf activity and of the assumed CCF gain transfer from HARPS to a 30-m class instrument; (ii) place the result against alternative detection strategies; (iii) temper the habitability/liquid-water language; (iv) fix the typographical and equation errors. With those additions the candidate-list output is a serviceable contribution, but the paper currently rests on a single prior measurement and a chain of unquantified assumptions that do not yet earn strong endorsement.
